    backoff=rs.Backoff.exponential(2.0, max_delay=60, jitter=0.25),
    retry_on=rs.RetryOn.TRANSIENT,
))
def fetch_from_flaky_api() -> dict:
    ...

A failed attempt emits a StepRetry event (visible in the run timeline), waits out the backoff, and re-executes. Failure hooks fire only when the budget is exhausted — not per attempt. Downstream steps are skipped only if the final attempt fails.

items.title: RetryPolicy
items.text:
rs.RetryPolicy(
    max_retries=3,          # retry budget after the initial attempt
    backoff=...,            # wait schedule; None = retry immediately
    retry_on=...,           # which failures are eligible (default: ALL)
    escalate=...,           # grow compute on OOM retries (Kubernetes)
)

The policy attaches at three levels; the nearest one wins (total override, no field merging):

@rs.Asset(retry=rs.RetryPolicy(max_retries=5))     # 1. asset (highest)
def flaky(): ...

rs.Job("nightly", assets=[...], retry=...)          # 2. job default for its steps
rs.CodeRepository(..., default_retry_policy=...)    # 3. repo-wide default
repo.materialize([...], retry=...)                  # acts at the job level for that run

An action step is outside this chain: it retries only by its action's own retry= (none by default), because re-running a half-applied merge or delete is a different risk from re-running a materialize.

items.title: Backoff
items.text:
Backoff is built from named constructors — one per wait shape. Every shape takes a relative jitter (a fraction of the computed wait, so it scales with the delay) and most take a max_delay ceiling so growth can't run away:

rs.Backoff.constant(10)                                    # 10s every time
rs.Backoff.linear(step=30)                                 # 30s, 60s, 90s, …
rs.Backoff.exponential(1.0, max_delay=60, jitter=0.25)     # 1s, 2s, 4s… capped at 60s, ±25%
rs.Backoff.fixed([10, 60, 300])                            # explicit schedule, clamps at 300s

The deterministic wait before the attempt that follows the n-th failure:

constructor wait constant(delay) delay linear(step, initial=0) initial + step * n exponential(initial, factor=2) initial * factor**(n-1) fixed(schedule) schedule[min(n-1, len-1)]

Cap and jitter apply uniformly: wait = min(computed, max_delay) * uniform(1-jitter, 1+jitter).

items.title: What gets retried: retry_on
items.text:
Two presets cover the common intents:

  • RetryOn.ALL (default) — any failure except cancellation.
  • RetryOn.TRANSIENT — only out-of-memory, timeout, and infrastructure failures. A deterministic ValueError fails identically every attempt; retrying it just burns compute.

For precise control, pass an allow-list mixing exception types and failure reasons:

@rs.Asset(retry=rs.RetryPolicy(
    max_retries=4,
    retry_on=[ConnectionError, vendor.RateLimitError, rs.FailureReason.OUT_OF_MEMORY],
))
def call_external(): ...

Exception types match subclass-aware, like an except clause — listing ConnectionError also catches ConnectionResetError. FailureReason members cover failures that have no exception object at all (an OOM-killed pod leaves nothing to type-match). Cancellation is never retried regardless of policy.

items.title: Named policies
items.text:
Register policies once on the repository and reference them by name — the same pattern as named IO handlers:

repo = rs.CodeRepository(
    assets=[...],
    retries={
        "flaky_io": rs.RetryPolicy(max_retries=5, backoff=rs.Backoff.exponential(1.0, max_delay=30)),
        "big_data": rs.RetryPolicy(
            max_retries=3,
            retry_on=rs.RetryOn.TRANSIENT,
            escalate=rs.ComputeEscalation(factor=2.0, max_memory="64Gi"),
        ),
    },
    default_retry_policy="flaky_io",
)

@rs.Asset(retry="big_data")
def skewed_join(): ...

An unknown name fails at resolve() with the registered names listed — never silently at execution time. Each repository resolves the name against its own retries, so two repositories built from the same assets can give the name different policies.

items.title: OOM escalation on Kubernetes
items.text:
On the Kubernetes executor every step runs in its own pod, so a retry can re-launch the step with more memory:

@rs.Asset(retry=rs.RetryPolicy(
    max_retries=3,
    retry_on=rs.RetryOn.TRANSIENT,
    escalate=rs.ComputeEscalation(factor=2.0, max_memory="64Gi"),
))
def skewed_join(): ...

Starting from the executor's worker_memory (say 8Gi), an OOM-killed attempt relaunches at 16Gi, then 32Gi, then 64Gi — clamped at max_memory, which is required. A pod killed by the OOM killer never gets to write a failure event; the orchestrator detects the dead Job and classifies from pod status: an explicit OOMKilled termination reason is OUT_OF_MEMORY, while a bare kill signal (exit 137/143 without that reason — evictions, preemptions, node drains) is INFRASTRUCTURE and does not escalate. OOM detection therefore relies on the container runtime reporting OOMKilled (standard on containerd with cgroup v2); a runtime that surfaces an OOM as a bare exit 137 classifies it INFRASTRUCTURE instead. escalate implies its reasons are retriable, so you don't also have to list OUT_OF_MEMORY in retry_on.

Each attempt creates a fresh Job (-r2, -r3, … name suffixes — a finished K8s Job can't re-run). ComputeEscalation(cpu_factor=..., max_cpu=...) optionally grows CPU alongside memory.

On the in-process and parallel executors escalate is inert — a local Python process can't be handed more RAM than its host has. Timing-based retries work everywhere.

items.title: Executor behavior
items.text:
• in_process — attempts re-run inline; the backoff sleep releases the GIL.
  • parallel — a failed subprocess step is re-submitted to the worker pool. The exception raised in the worker is re-raised in the orchestrator, so exception-type retry_on lists match as usual.
  • kubernetes — attempts re-create the step Job; classification comes from the step's own failure event when it wrote one, or from pod status when it didn't. The step pod stamps the failure reason and the exception's class hierarchy onto its StepFailure event, so exception-type allow-lists match across the pod boundary. A pod killed before it can write an event (e.g. OOM) is classified from pod status alone — only reason-based matching applies there.

Concurrency slots (pools, the executor's step budget) are held per attempt: a non-zero backoff sleep releases them so waiting siblings (or other runs) can proceed, and re-claims them before the next attempt. Cancelling a run interrupts a backoff sleep within about a second on the in-process and parallel executors, and within a few seconds on Kubernetes (cancellation propagates through a per-run watcher).

Retry policies cover task and bash-task steps too (including a graph asset's internal tasks): declare one on the definition (@rs.Task(retry=...), BashTask(..., retry=...)) or let a job-level / repo-default policy fill steps that don't set their own.

items.title: Observability
items.text:
Every retried attempt leaves a StepRetry event on the run timeline carrying the attempt number, the classified failure reason, the next delay, and (when escalating) the next resource request:

metadata key example rivers/attempt 1 rivers/failure_reason out_of_memory rivers/next_delay_ms 5000 rivers/next_compute {"memory":"16Gi"}

The attempt count for a step is the number of its StepRetry events plus one; the final StepSuccess/StepFailure settles the outcome. Each failed attempt also stores its Python traceback. The run page shows the traceback of each failed step, and the asset page shows each attempt's on its StepRetry or StepFailure event.

items.title: Multi-assets
items.text:
A multi-asset is one function call producing several outputs, so it can only retry as a unit. The policy is declared on Asset.from_multi(retry=...) itself — like compute, it belongs to the step, not to an output:

@rs.Asset.from_multi(
    output_defs=[rs.AssetDef("orders"), rs.AssetDef("customers")],
    retry=rs.RetryPolicy(max_retries=3, retry_on=[ConnectionError]),
)
def load_tables():
    return {"orders": ..., "customers": ...}

Dict-returning multi-assets retry normally. Generator multi-assets do not retry: their body runs during output iteration, after earlier yields may already have materialized — re-running the whole generator would double-write those outputs.

Graph assets take Asset.from_graph(retry=...) for the step carrying the graph asset's name. A graph's internal tasks are independent steps — give them their own @rs.Task(retry=...) policies; on the Kubernetes executor each internal task pod then retries on its own ladder.

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• Generator-style multi-assets don't retry (see above); dict-returning ones do.
  • A Kubernetes pod killed before it can write its failure event (OOM kill, eviction) is classified from pod status alone — exception-type allow-lists can't match there, only failure reasons.
  • Cancelling a run mid-backoff takes effect within about a second on the local executors and within a few seconds on Kubernetes — not instantly.

items.title: Scheduling & Automation
items.text: rivers runs assets in three ways outside of a manual repo.materialize() call: schedules (time-based), sensors (event-based), and automation conditions (graph-state-based). All three are evaluated by the rivers daemon, share the same run-launch path, and can coexist on the same repository.

items.title: Three trigger models
items.text:
Trigger Drives runs based on Defined on Best for Schedule A cron expression A job "Run job X every day at 2am." Sensor A polling function that returns run requests A job "Run job X when a new file appears in this S3 prefix." AutomationCondition The state of an asset and its deps An asset "Materialize this asset whenever any of its deps update, but not while it's in progress."

The three are not mutually exclusive — a repository can ship all of them at once. They differ in what causes a run to fire, not in how the run is executed.

items.title: Schedules
items.text:
A Schedule is a cron expression bound to a job. The decorated function — the evaluation function — runs on each tick and returns a RunRequest (or SkipReason, or a list of either).

import rivers as rs

@rs.Schedule(cron_schedule="0 2 * * *", job_name="nightly")
def nightly_etl(context: rs.ScheduleEvaluationContext):
    return rs.RunRequest(
        run_key=context.scheduled_execution_time,   # idempotent across daemon restarts
        tags={"trigger": "scheduled"},
    )

A schedule's evaluation function may also yield a BackfillRequest to launch a multi-partition backfill instead of a single run, or a SkipReason("…") to skip the tick. See the Schedules API reference for the full signature.

Cron expressions accept 5 fields (min hour dom mon dow) or 6 fields (sec min hour dom mon dow); seconds are optional.

items.title: Sensors
items.text:
A Sensor is an evaluation function that the daemon re-runs on a fixed cadence (minimum_interval) — typically polling an external system. The function returns run requests when it detects work to do.

@rs.Sensor(job_name="ingest", minimum_interval="30s")
def s3_inbox(context: rs.SensorEvaluationContext):
    last_seen = context.cursor or "1970-01-01"
    new_files = list_s3_files_after(last_seen)
    if not new_files:
        return rs.SkipReason("inbox empty")
    return rs.SensorResult(
        run_requests=[rs.RunRequest(tags={"file": f}) for f in new_files],
        cursor=new_files[-1],   # persisted for the next tick
    )

Sensors maintain a cursor — an opaque string the daemon persists between ticks. Use it to track "what's the last thing I've already processed"; the next tick receives it back via context.cursor.

For idempotency, set run_key= on the RunRequest — the run-queue de-dupes across runs that share a key.

items.title: Automation conditions
items.text:
AutomationCondition is a declarative DSL that fires on asset graph state, not on time or external events. You attach a condition to an asset; the daemon evaluates it on every tick and materializes the asset when the condition is true.

@rs.Asset(automation_condition=rs.AutomationCondition.eager())
def hourly_aggregate(raw_events: list) -> int:
    return len(raw_events)

eager() is the most common preset — "materialize when any dep updates, skip while a dep is in progress, and don't refire while already in flight (a run or an active backfill)." Other presets:

  • on_cron("0 * * * *") — fire on a cron schedule, but only after every dep has updated since the last cron tick. Won't overlap a run that's still in flight.
  • on_missing() — fire once when the asset becomes missing, then stop.

You can also build conditions from leaf primitives (missing(), code_version_changed(), any_deps_updated(), etc.) using & / | / ~. See the Automation API reference for the full operator catalog.

Unlike schedules and sensors, automation conditions don't go through RunRequests — the daemon launches matching assets directly via the run coordinator.

items.title: Picking between them
items.text:
The three triggers overlap. A rough decision rule:

  • You know the time the run should happen → Schedule with a cron.
  • An external system knows when there's work → Sensor polling that system.
  • The graph itself knows when there's work (deps just updated, code changed, partition is missing) → AutomationCondition on the asset.

AutomationCondition.on_cron() looks like a schedule but isn't — the difference is who decides the run should happen. A Schedule always fires on the cron tick; on_cron() waits for both the tick and every dep to be ready, so it's the right choice for cron-driven downstreams in a partitioned graph.

items.title: Daemon execution
items.text:
All three triggers are evaluated by the same background process: AutomationDaemon. It is started in-process by rivers dev and rivers serve, and tested directly via the AutomationDaemon constructor. The daemon:

  1. Loads each schedule, sensor, and automation condition tree from the repository.
  2. For schedules, computes the next cron tick; for sensors, polls every minimum_interval; for automation conditions, re-evaluates every condition_eval_interval (default 30s).
  3. Calls the evaluation function (in-process, in a thread, or in a subprocess — see below).
  4. Persists a tick record (run requests, skip reason, cursor, error) to storage.
  5. Submits any resulting runs through the run queue.

items.title: Eval modes
items.text:
Schedule and Sensor accept an eval_mode argument:

Mode Behavior EvalMode.Auto (default) Auto-detected at daemon start: async functions run automatically on the Python event loop managed from Rust; sync functions run on a dedicated thread. EvalMode.InProcess Same as Auto today — keep the function in the daemon process. EvalMode.Subprocess Run in a loky subprocess, which rebuilds the resources from their field values, secrets included. Useful when the eval function needs CPU isolation or is unsafe to run alongside the daemon.

Automation conditions don't have an eval mode — they are evaluated entirely in Rust (no user code runs unless an asset matches and gets launched).

items.title: Cursor and tick history
items.text:
The daemon persists every tick to storage:

  • repo.storage.get_ticks(name, limit=...) returns the recent tick history for a schedule, sensor, or automation condition (capped at max_ticks_retained, default 100).
  • A sensor's last cursor is read back on the next tick, surviving daemon restarts.

items.title: Disabling triggers
items.text:
Both Schedule and Sensor accept default_status=ScheduleStatus.Stopped / SensorStatus.Stopped. Stopped triggers are registered (their definitions are validated, and the UI shows them) but the daemon doesn't tick them. This is the recommended default during development — rivers dev doesn't kick off every job the moment you save the file.

Triggers can also be paused/resumed at runtime via the UI.

items.title: Resource and config injection
items.text: Schedule and sensor evaluation functions receive the same resource/config injection as asset functions: any parameter name matching a registered resource is injected, and the typed ScheduleEvaluationContext[ConfigT] / SensorEvaluationContext[ConfigT] makes a Pydantic config available on context.config. See Configuration and Resources for details.

items.title: Programmatic evaluation (for tests)
items.text:
You don't need to start the daemon to test a schedule or sensor. CodeRepository exposes:

result = repo.evaluate_schedule("nightly_etl")
result = repo.evaluate_sensor("s3_inbox", cursor="2024-01-01", last_tick_time=1234.5)

Both return a tick result with the run requests / skip reason / cursor your function produced — without dispatching anything. Use these in unit tests to assert your evaluation logic without standing up the daemon.

For automation conditions, use the daemon directly (AutomationDaemon(repo, storage).start() in a test fixture), since condition evaluation is owned by the Rust daemon path.

items.title: What it did
items.text:
A toggle in the lineage page topbar (Since last deploy) that when on:

  1. Highlighted nodes whose code version changed in the last deploy with a NEW chip (top-right of the capsule) + primary-color ring around the node.
  2. Highlighted edges touching any changed node with the primary color + flowing gradient animation; dimmed all other edges.
  3. Dimmed nodes that existed before the deploy.
  4. Surfaced a small inline chip next to the toggle showing the deploy sha + relative time (e.g. deploy · 610e0a1 · a few minutes ago).

It matched Rivers' LineageGraphScreen "deployView" toggle + deploy-diff banner (rivers-screens.jsx:1181-1205, :1242-1259).

items.title: Why it was removed
items.text: The "changed subset" was synthesized — we picked every 3rd node deterministically because storage doesn't yet track which assets shipped in which deploy. Showing fake deploy deltas is worse than showing none, so the toggle was cut.

items.title: What needs to land before reintroducing
items.text:
1. Deploy recording: storage needs to persist each materialize of the code location with a sha + timestamp + author, and track which asset code_version values changed since the previous deploy.
  2. Server fn: get_last_deploy() -> Option<DeployRecord> returning { sha, when, by, added: Vec<key>, changed: Vec<key>, removed: Vec<key> }.
  3. Feature gate: since the commercial angle is deploy auditing + drift detection, gate the UI toggle + the server fn behind the enterprise feature flag (whatever mechanism we pick for that layer — likely a build-time cfg or runtime license check).

items.title: Sketch of the reintroduction
items.text:
// graph.rs
let (deploy_view, set_deploy_view) = signal(false);
let last_deploy = Resource::new(|| (), |_| get_last_deploy());

// Topbar toggle
<label class="toggle-label" title="Highlight assets changed since the last deploy">
    <input type="checkbox" prop:checked=... on:change=... />
    "Since last deploy"
</label>
<Show when=move || deploy_view.get()>
    {move || last_deploy.get().and_then(|r| r.ok()).flatten().map(|d| view! {
        <span class="deploy-pill">{format!("deploy · {} · {}", d.sha, d.when)}</span>
    })}
</Show>

// DagGraph wiring
let changed = if deploy_view.get() {
    last_deploy.get().and_then(|r| r.ok()).flatten()
        .map(|d| d.changed.into_iter().collect::<HashSet<_>>())
        .unwrap_or_default()
} else {
    HashSet::new()
};
<DagGraph ... changed_keys=changed />

items.title: Airbyte
items.text: rivers.integrations.airbyte runs Airbyte syncs as rivers assets. AirbyteResource calls the Airbyte API. Its connection_asset method makes a multi-asset for an Airbyte connection, with one output per enabled stream. A run starts a sync job, waits for it, and records a materialization for each stream.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
The integration needs no extra: it calls the Airbyte API with the Python standard library.

Create an application in Airbyte (Settings → Applications) to get a client id and a client secret. AirbyteResource reads them from AIRBYTE_CLIENT_ID and AIRBYTE_CLIENT_SECRET, and connects to Airbyte Cloud:

from rivers.integrations.airbyte import AirbyteResource

airbyte = AirbyteResource()  # Airbyte Cloud, credentials from AIRBYTE_CLIENT_ID and AIRBYTE_CLIENT_SECRET

For a self-managed Airbyte, set the URLs of its two APIs:

airbyte = AirbyteResource(
    api_url="http://localhost:8000/api/public/v1",
    configuration_api_url="http://localhost:8000/api/v1",
)

With basic authentication, set username and password instead of the client credentials. Without authentication, set neither.

Fields that you do not give are read from AIRBYTE_* environment variables, for example AIRBYTE_API_URL.

Field Default Description api_url "https://api.airbyte.com/v1" The Airbyte API. Self-managed: <host>/api/public/v1. configuration_api_url "https://cloud.airbyte.com/api/v1" Airbyte's Configuration API, for the per-stream counts. Self-managed: <host>/api/v1. client_id, client_secret None Application credentials. The resource gets an access token with them, and gets a new one 30 s before it expires. username, password None Basic authentication, for a self-managed Airbyte. request_timeout 15 Seconds to wait for each API response. request_max_retries 3 Retries of a request that fails with a connection error, HTTP 429, or HTTP 5xx. Other HTTP errors fail at once. request_retry_delay 0.25 Seconds between retries. poll_interval 10 Seconds between status checks of a running job. poll_timeout None Seconds to wait for a job. None waits until the job finishes. cancel_on_interrupt True Cancel the job when rivers stops waiting before the job finishes. See Timeouts and cancel.

items.title: Assets for a connection
items.text:
import rivers as rs

postgres = airbyte.get_connection("9924bcd0-99be-453d-ba47-c2c9766f7da5")

repo = rs.CodeRepository(
    assets=[airbyte.connection_asset(postgres)],
    resources={"airbyte": airbyte},
)

get_connection reads the connection and its enabled streams from the Airbyte API. connection_asset makes a multi-asset named airbyte_ and the connection name in snake case, for example airbyte_postgres_to_snowflake. Each output has the name of its destination table: the connection's table prefix and the stream name, for example pg_users. The outputs have the kind airbyte.

get_connection runs each time a process loads the code location, for example each Kubernetes step pod. To load the code location without the Airbyte API, for example in tests, save the connection as JSON and read it back:

from pathlib import Path
from rivers.integrations.airbyte import AirbyteConnection

Path("airbyte/postgres.json").write_text(postgres.model_dump_json())  # once

postgres = AirbyteConnection.model_validate_json(Path("airbyte/postgres.json").read_text())

When the connection's streams change in Airbyte, load the code location again to update the outputs.

items.title: The registered resource
items.text:
A run uses the resource registered under the key airbyte, not the instance that made the asset. So a run can override the resource's fields, from Python or from the launch dialog in the UI:

repo.materialize(config={"resources": {"airbyte": {"poll_timeout": 7200}}})

Without the resource, the code location fails to load with unresolved input 'airbyte'.

To register a resource under another key, for example for a second Airbyte, give the key as resource_key:

local = AirbyteResource(
    api_url="http://localhost:8000/api/public/v1",
    configuration_api_url="http://localhost:8000/api/v1",
)
mysql = local.get_connection("0c31738c-0b2d-4887-b506-e2cd1c39cc35")

repo = rs.CodeRepository(
    assets=[
        airbyte.connection_asset(postgres),
        local.connection_asset(mysql, resource_key="airbyte_local"),
    ],
    resources={"airbyte": airbyte, "airbyte_local": local},
)

items.title: What a run does
items.text:
1. Reads the connection again, to find streams that were removed or added after the code location loaded.
  2. Starts one sync job for the whole connection.
  3. Checks the job every poll_interval seconds until it finishes.
  4. Records a materialization for each selected output.

The asset's function is async, so its step waits for the job without holding a worker of the executor, and the Airbyte assets of one level wait at the same time: all of them with the parallel executor (max_async_concurrent limits them), and up to four with the in-process executor. A waiting step keeps its pool slots until the job finishes.

Airbyte syncs all the streams of a connection. A run that selects some outputs syncs all the streams too, and records materializations only for the selected outputs.

When the job fails or is cancelled in Airbyte, all the outputs fail with AirbyteError. When a selected output's stream is no longer enabled, that output fails and the others succeed. A stream that was enabled after the code location loaded is synced, and the run log names it.

When a sync of the connection is already running, Airbyte does not start another, and the run fails with AirbyteError (HTTP 409).

Each materialization has this metadata:

Key Type Description airbyte/connection_id str The connection id. airbyte/job_id int The Airbyte job id. airbyte/stream str The stream: namespace.name, or the name when the stream has no namespace. airbyte/records_committed int Records the job committed for this stream. airbyte/bytes_committed MetadataValue.bytes Bytes the job committed for this stream.

The counts come from the Configuration API, because the Airbyte API reports only totals for the whole job. When Airbyte has no counts for a stream, its materialization has no count keys. When the Configuration API request fails, no materialization has counts, and the run log has a warning.

items.title: Timeouts and cancel
items.text:
Set poll_timeout to stop waiting for long jobs:

airbyte = AirbyteResource(poll_timeout=3600)

When rivers stops waiting before the job finishes, it cancels the job in Airbyte. This occurs after poll_timeout, when an API request fails, and on an interrupt such as Ctrl-C. Set cancel_on_interrupt=False to let the job continue in Airbyte. A process that is killed, for example a deleted Kubernetes pod, cannot cancel the job.

To try a failed sync again, give the asset a retry policy:

from rivers.integrations.airbyte import AirbyteError

airbyte.connection_asset(postgres, retry=rs.RetryPolicy(max_retries=2, retry_on=[AirbyteError]))

items.title: Change the outputs
items.text:
asset_def_fn makes the rs.AssetDef of each stream. It takes the AirbyteConnection and one of its AirbyteStreams. connection.output_def(stream, ...) returns the default output with the fields that you give. The other keyword arguments of connection_asset go to rs.Asset.from_multi, for example group, hooks, automation_condition, or retry:

postgres_sync = airbyte.connection_asset(
    postgres,
    name="postgres_sync",
    asset_def_fn=lambda connection, stream: connection.output_def(
        stream, kinds=["airbyte", "snowflake"]
    ),
    group="raw",
    automation_condition=rs.AutomationCondition.on_cron("0 2 * * *"),
)

The default output sets only the name, so it gets group and the kind airbyte from connection_asset. A field that asset_def_fn sets replaces them: above, the outputs have the kinds airbyte and snowflake.

Two streams with the same name in different namespaces need an asset_def_fn that gives them different names, for example with stream.namespace.

items.title: Downstream assets
items.text:
Airbyte writes the tables, and each run records a Materialization, so rivers stores no values for these assets. Declare the dependency with rs.AssetDef.dep, and read the table from the destination:

@rs.Asset(deps=[rs.AssetDef.dep("pg_users")])
def active_users() -> None:
    ...  # query pg_users in the destination

items.title: Start a sync in your own code
items.text:
sync starts a sync job, waits for it, and returns the AirbyteJob. It raises AirbyteError when the job does not succeed. Take the registered resource as a parameter, so that a run's config reaches it too:

@rs.Asset
def postgres_rows(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext, airbyte: AirbyteResource) -> int:
    job = airbyte.sync("9924bcd0-99be-453d-ba47-c2c9766f7da5", log=context.log)
    return job.rows_synced  # records of all streams

In an async def asset, use async_sync. It takes the same arguments and waits without blocking the event loop.

See the API reference for all the classes.

items.title: Authentication (OIDC & forward auth)
items.text:
The rivers UI supports three authentication modes:

Mode What it does none (default) No authentication — today's behavior. Fine for rivers dev and network-isolated clusters. oidc The UI runs the OpenID Connect authorization-code flow (with PKCE) against your identity provider directly. No proxy required. forward A reverse proxy in front of rivers authenticates (Authelia, Authentik, oauth2-proxy, Envoy Gateway, …) and rivers trusts the identity headers it injects — but only from peers on an explicit trusted-proxy CIDR list.

In both enabled modes, every route except /healthz, /readyz, and the sign-in endpoints (/auth/login, /auth/callback, /auth/logout) requires an identity: pages, server functions, the live-event stream, and debug endpoints. Manual launches (materialize, job runs, reruns, backfills) record who triggered them — the run's launched_by carries the user's stable subject plus email/name snapshots, shown in the runs list and detail pages.

Configuration is env-var driven (RIVERS_AUTH_*); on Kubernetes the Helm chart maps ui.auth.* values onto those env vars, with secrets flowing via secretKeyRef only.

items.title: OIDC
items.text:
Register a client at your IdP with redirect URI <publicUrl>/auth/callback, then:

# values.yaml
ui:
  auth:
    mode: oidc
    publicUrl: https://rivers.example.com
    oidc:
      issuer: https://keycloak.example.com/realms/main
      clientId: rivers
      existingSecret: rivers-oidc-client   # key: client-secret

kubectl create secret generic rivers-oidc-client \
  --from-literal=client-secret='<client secret>' -n rivers
helm upgrade rivers ./deploy/helm/rivers -f values.yaml

Any spec-compliant IdP works via issuer discovery — Keycloak, Okta, Entra ID, Google, Dex, Authentik, Zitadel. Knobs:

Value Env var Default ui.auth.publicUrl RIVERS_AUTH_PUBLIC_URL — (required) ui.auth.oidc.issuer RIVERS_AUTH_OIDC_ISSUER — (required) ui.auth.oidc.clientId RIVERS_AUTH_OIDC_CLIENT_ID — (required) ui.auth.oidc.existingSecret RIVERS_AUTH_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET — (required unless publicClient: true) ui.auth.oidc.scopes RIVERS_AUTH_OIDC_SCOPES openid profile email ui.auth.oidc.groupsClaim RIVERS_AUTH_OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM groups (dotted paths traverse, e.g. realm_access.roles) ui.auth.oidc.rpLogout RIVERS_AUTH_OIDC_RP_LOGOUT false — when true, sign-out also ends the IdP session ui.auth.sessionTtl RIVERS_AUTH_SESSION_TTL 28800 (8h)

The issuer's TLS certificate is validated against both the container's system trust store and bundled public CA roots, so an IdP served with an internal or corporate CA works once that CA is in the image's trust store (the standard ca-certificates path); public IdPs need no setup.

Sessions are stateless encrypted cookies (AES-256-GCM) — no session table, no sticky sessions, and no OAuth tokens are ever stored. The cookie key is chart-managed (rivers-ui-auth Secret, generated once and preserved across upgrades) or brought via ui.auth.cookieSecret.existingSecret; the value must be base64 of at least 32 bytes. Rotating it signs every user out at once. When the session expires the next page load transparently re-runs the redirect — invisible while the IdP session is alive.

Outside the chart (docker-compose, bare processes), set RIVERS_AUTH_COOKIE_SECRET explicitly — e.g. openssl rand -base64 48. Without it each process generates an ephemeral key at startup (logged as a warning): sessions die on every restart, and behind a load balancer each replica mints cookies the others can't decrypt, so logins bounce back to the IdP indefinitely.

items.title: Forward auth
items.text:
The proxy owns login; rivers consumes the identity headers it injects. Requests are only trusted when the socket peer is inside trustedProxies (never X-Forwarded-For, which is spoofable). A request from any other peer gets 403 with its identity headers ignored; a request from a trusted proxy without identity headers gets a diagnostic 401 — that means the proxy authenticated nothing or drops its auth response headers.

The proxy must strip inbound identity headers

rivers trusts every Remote-User/Remote-Email/Remote-Groups/ Remote-Name line on a request from a trusted peer — it cannot tell a proxy-set header from one the client sent. Your proxy must replace (strip-then-set), not merely append, these headers. A proxy that only adds its own values while forwarding the client's copies lets any authenticated user send Remote-Groups: admins and pass the group allowlist. Most forwardAuth integrations set (replace) the response headers, but verify: ingress-nginx auth-response-headers and Traefik authResponseHeaders overwrite; if you hand-configure header passing, ensure inbound Remote-* are dropped at the edge.

ui:
  auth:
    mode: forward
    forward:
      # The proxy pods' addresses ONLY — as narrow as you can make it.
      trustedProxies: ["10.42.3.14/32"]
      logoutUrl: https://auth.example.com/logout

trustedProxies matches the source IP of the connection rivers receives, so it must name the proxy's real peer addresses. There are two sound ways to set it.

Pin the proxy's IPs (shown above) — its static egress IPs, a dedicated node pool's range, or /32s kept current by your tooling. Simple, but proxy pods reschedule onto other nodes and get new pod IPs, so pinned /32s go stale.

Trust broadly, gate with a NetworkPolicy (recommended). Make network reachability the boundary instead of the IP list: a NetworkPolicy that admits UI traffic only from the proxy pods — matched by label, which survives rescheduling — and then open trustedProxies wide. The IP check is now coarse on purpose, because nothing but the proxy can even open a connection:

# values.yaml — trust any peer; the NetworkPolicy below is the real gate
ui:
  auth:
    forward:
      trustedProxies: ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"]   # ::/0 only needed on dual-stack

…paired with a NetworkPolicy applied alongside the release (kubectl apply / your GitOps), pinning UI ingress to the proxy pods by label:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: rivers-ui-proxy-only
  namespace: rivers
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: rivers-ui }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: envoy-gateway-system }
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app.kubernetes.io/name: envoy }   # your proxy's labels
      ports: [{ port: 3000 }]

This is the standard forward-auth posture — the app is unreachable except through the proxy — and it needs a policy-enforcing CNI (k3s ships one; plain flannel does not, so the policy would silently no-op there).

A broad range with no NetworkPolicy is an impersonation hole

0.0.0.0/0 — or the pod CIDR (k3s defaults to 10.42.0.0/16) — with no network control lets any pod in the cluster forge Remote-* headers and impersonate any user. Broad trustedProxies is only safe paired with the NetworkPolicy above (or equivalent isolation).

Header names default to the Authelia/Authentik convention and are all configurable:

Proxy Values to set Authelia / Authentik defaults work (Remote-User, Remote-Email, Remote-Groups, Remote-Name) oauth2-proxy (--set-xauthrequest) userHeader: X-Auth-Request-User, emailHeader: X-Auth-Request-Email, groupsHeader: X-Auth-Request-Groups Cloudflare Access userHeader: Cf-Access-Authenticated-User-Email, emailHeader: same Envoy Gateway (gateway-native OIDC) whatever your claimToHeaders maps emit — see below

items.title: Envoy Gateway + Keycloak
items.text:
The chart already ships an HTTPRoute (ui.httpRoute.enabled), so Envoy Gateway can run the OIDC flow itself and mint identity headers from validated token claims:

apiVersion: gateway.envoyproxy.io/v1alpha1
kind: SecurityPolicy
metadata:
  name: rivers-ui-auth
spec:
  targetRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: HTTPRoute
      name: rivers-ui
  oidc:
    provider:
      issuer: https://keycloak.example.com/realms/main
    clientID: rivers
    clientSecret:
      name: rivers-oidc-client
    forwardAccessToken: true
  jwt:
    providers:
      - name: keycloak
        remoteJWKS:
          uri: https://keycloak.example.com/realms/main/protocol/openid-connect/certs
        claimToHeaders:
          - claim: sub          # stable id → UserRef.subject
            header: x-user
          - claim: email
            header: x-user-email
          - claim: preferred_username
            header: x-user-name

ui:
  auth:
    mode: forward
    forward:
      trustedProxies: ["10.42.7.5/32"]   # the Envoy proxy pods only — never the pod CIDR
      userHeader: x-user
      emailHeader: x-user-email
      nameHeader: x-user-name

Map sub (not preferred_username) to the user header so the stored subject is the never-reassigned Keycloak UUID. One inherited limit: Envoy's claimToHeaders only extracts primitive claims — array claims like Keycloak's groups cannot become a header, so enforce group-based access at the gateway (its JWT claim authorization matches arrays via valueType: StringArray) or use rivers' native oidc mode instead.

items.title: Traefik + Authelia / ingress-nginx
items.text:
Any forwardAuth-style setup works unchanged — configure the proxy to copy the auth service's response headers onto the request:

  • Traefik: a forwardAuth middleware with authResponseHeaders: [Remote-User, Remote-Email, Remote-Groups, Remote-Name].
  • ingress-nginx: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-url + auth-response-headers: Remote-User,Remote-Email,Remote-Groups,Remote-Name.

Then set trustedProxies to the controller pods' addresses (see the warning above — not the cluster pod CIDR). If the UI Service is reachable without traversing the proxy, forward mode is an auth bypass — pair it with a NetworkPolicy.

items.title: Access control
items.text:
Optional allowlists apply in both modes; empty lists admit any authenticated user, and a match in any list admits:

ui:
  auth:
    allowedDomains: ["example.com"]      # email domain
    allowedGroups: ["data-eng"]          # from the groups claim / header
    allowedUsers: ["ops@example.com"]    # email or subject

Email-based rules (allowedDomains, and allowedUsers matched by email) only trust the OIDC email claim when the IdP marks it verified (email_verified: true) — an unverified address is ignored for access control and identity. For IdPs that don't assert email_verified, gate on allowedGroups or on allowedUsers by subject instead.

Denied users get a 403 page naming the identity and the gate. Finer roles (viewer/launcher/admin, per-code-location grants) are a planned follow-up on top of the groups already captured in the session.

Allowlists are enforced on every request, but the identity they check — subject, email, and groups — is snapshotted into the session cookie at sign-in. To keep the cookie small, only the groups that match the allowlist at sign-in time are stored. Consequences:

  • Removing a user from the allowlist (or from a group) — and any IdP-side change like disabling the account — takes hold at the next sign-in, so at most sessionTtl (default 8h) later. To evict everyone immediately, rotate the cookie secret (signs all sessions out at once).
  • Tightening allowedGroups/allowedDomains/allowedUsers locks existing sessions out on their next request.
  • Adding a group to allowedGroups only admits existing sessions after they sign in again (that group wasn't stored in their cookie). Expanding allowedDomains/allowedUsers is immediate — email and subject are stored in full.

Pick a sessionTtl that matches how fast access changes must propagate.

items.title: Who launched what
items.text:
With auth enabled, manual actions carry the acting user end-to-end: the UI stamps the session identity onto the gRPC launch request, the code location persists it on the run's launched_by (and on backfill records), and the UI renders "manual · \<user>". From Python:

record = storage.get_run(run_id)
assert record.launched_by.kind == "manual"
if record.launched_by.user is not None:
    print(record.launched_by.user.subject, record.launched_by.user.display)

status = repo.get_backfill(backfill_id)
print(status.launched_by.kind, status.launched_by.user)

Runs from schedules, sensors, conditions, and the Python API (repo.materialize(), Job.execute()) are unaffected — Python-launched runs have user = None until API tokens land.

items.title: Local development
items.text:
rivers dev defaults to mode: none. To exercise OIDC locally, run an IdP (e.g. Dex or Keycloak in Docker) and export the env vars before starting:

export RIVERS_AUTH_MODE=oidc
export RIVERS_AUTH_PUBLIC_URL=http://localhost:3000
export RIVERS_AUTH_OIDC_ISSUER=http://localhost:5556
export RIVERS_AUTH_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=rivers
export RIVERS_AUTH_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=...
rivers dev my_module

Forward mode is testable with plain curl:

RIVERS_AUTH_MODE=forward \
RIVERS_AUTH_FORWARD_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1/32 \
rivers dev my_module
# A request without the identity header is rejected by the gate:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:3000/                          # 401
# Add the header a trusted proxy would inject, and the same request is admitted:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H 'Remote-User: jdoe' http://127.0.0.1:3000/   # not 401

items.title: Class-Based Assets
items.text:
Every asset can be defined as a class instead of a decorated function. The class body lists what the asset is and does: its configuration as class attributes, its verbs as classmethods. Subclass one of the four bases — rs.Asset, rs.MultiAsset, rs.GraphAsset, rs.ExternalAsset — and register the class directly:

import rivers as rs


class Orders(rs.Asset):
    io_handler = delta_handler
    kinds = "table"
    group = "sales"

    @classmethod
    def materialize(cls, ctx: rs.AssetExecutionContext):
        return load_orders()


repo = rs.CodeRepository(assets=[Orders])

Both forms produce the same objects — a class desugars at registration into exactly what the decorator form builds, so resolution, execution, scheduling, and the UI see no difference. Use whichever reads better; mix them freely in one repository.

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• Methods are @classmethod. This is mechanical, not style: the parallel executor re-imports Module.Class.method in worker processes, and a bound classmethod needs no instance lifecycle. A plain def materialize(self) is rejected at registration — its first parameter would be read as a dependency.
  • The asset name is the snake_cased class name (EnrichedOrders → enriched_orders); a name = "..." class attribute overrides it.
  • Configuration attributes map to the decorator parameters of the same kind: io_handler, tags, kinds, group, code_version, metadata, partitions_def, deps, hooks, automation_condition, pool, retry, compute, … Each is a typed attribute on the base classes, so your editor autocompletes them inside the class body and a type checker flags wrong value types (kinds = 123). The kinds don't all accept the same set — Asset.from_multi() takes no pool, ExternalAsset takes no retry, and so on; declaring one a kind can't carry is a registration-time error rather than a silent drop.
  • Actions are @rs.action classmethods in the body, or an actions = [...] list of AssetAction objects, mirroring the decorator's actions= argument.
  • Dependencies are materialize parameters, exactly as in the decorator form.
  • Registration is explicit — CodeRepository(assets=[Orders]). Desugaring happens there, not at class creation, so defining a class has no import-time side effects.

items.title: Sharing through inheritance
items.text:
Shared configuration and helpers live in base classes. A base class is just a class — it only becomes an asset if you list it in assets=[...]:

class WarehouseAsset(rs.Asset):
    """Shared handler + plumbing for every warehouse table."""

    io_handler = delta_handler

    @classmethod
    def _clean(cls, df):        # helper — not a verb, ignored by registration
        return df.drop_nulls()


class Orders(WarehouseAsset):
    @classmethod
    def materialize(cls, ctx):
        return cls._clean(load_orders())


class Customers(WarehouseAsset):
    group = "crm"               # subclass attributes override base ones

    @classmethod
    def materialize(cls, ctx):
        return cls._clean(load_customers())

Fifty Delta-backed assets inherit the handler by naming their base class. Standard MRO rules apply: the most derived definition of an attribute or verb wins. A materialize defined on the base is inherited too — cls binds to the subclass, in-process and in parallel workers alike, so template bases can parameterize by class attributes:

class TableSnapshot(rs.Asset):
    table = ""

    @classmethod
    def materialize(cls, ctx):
        return snapshot(cls.table)


class UsersSnapshot(TableSnapshot):
    table = "users"


class OrdersSnapshot(TableSnapshot):
    table = "orders"

Listing a class with no executable verb (materialize / observe / compose) is a registration-time error — that's what distinguishes an accidentally listed mixin from an asset.

items.title: The other three kinds
items.text:
Multi assets gain the most: outputs are attributes, so names aren't repeated as strings and per-output configuration sits next to the name it configures. An output whose AssetDef has no name= takes the attribute name (the AssetDef itself is not changed); an explicit name= wins:

class Ingest(rs.MultiAsset):
    customers = rs.AssetDef(io_handler=delta_customers)
    orders = rs.AssetDef(io_handler=delta_orders, group="sales")

    @classmethod
    def materialize(cls, ctx):
        yield rs.Output(load_customers(), output_name="customers")
        yield rs.Output(load_orders(), output_name="orders")

Graph assets define compose, traced under the composition context exactly like the decorator form:

class ValidatedPipeline(rs.GraphAsset):
    io_handler = output_io

    @classmethod
    def compose(cls, enriched_orders: dict):
        validate_data(enriched_orders)
        return compute_margins(enriched_orders)

External assets define observe (optional — a verb-less external is a plain reference to data produced elsewhere):

class VendorFeed(rs.ExternalAsset):
    io_handler = feed_handler

    @classmethod
    def observe(cls, ctx) -> rs.Observation:
        return rs.Observation(metadata={"rows": rs.MetadataValue.int(1)}, data_version=etag())

External assets are observed, not produced — defining materialize on an ExternalAsset subclass is an error; model data you operate on as a regular asset.

items.title: Actions
items.text:
The class body lists every verb the asset supports — materialize plus any actions, marked with @rs.action. Shared verbs inherit through base classes like everything else, and a subclass override replaces the inherited action:

class TableMaintenance(rs.Asset):
    io_handler = WAREHOUSE

    @rs.action(outcome=rs.Outcome.Unchanged, concurrency=rs.ActionConcurrency.Exclusive)
    @classmethod
    def optimize(cls, ctx: rs.ActionContext) -> None: ...

    @rs.action(outcome=rs.Outcome.Unchanged, concurrency=rs.ActionConcurrency.Exclusive)
    @classmethod
    def vacuum(cls, ctx: rs.ActionContext) -> None: ...


class Orders(TableMaintenance):  # inherits optimize + vacuum
    @classmethod
    def materialize(cls, ctx) -> pl.DataFrame: ...

Delta tables don't need hand-written maintenance verbs: DeltaAsset ships optimize, vacuum, and delete built in, declared per the conventional verbs table.

Reusable AssetAction objects can also be assigned as class attributes (optimize = delta_optimize) or listed in actions = [...]. A list entry belongs to the class that holds the list, so the most derived class that declares a verb wins either way. A class that gives one verb two different definitions, one in its list and one as an attribute, is a registration-time error. Shadowing an inherited action with a non-action attribute is a registration-time error, not a silent removal.

items.title: Jobs and selections
items.text:
Jobs accept the classes anywhere an asset instance is accepted; a multi-asset class expands to its output names:

rs.Job(name="nightly", assets=[Orders, Ingest])

items.title: Parallel execution
items.text: Class-form assets work across the loky process boundary by reference: workers re-import the defining module and rebuild the IO handler from the class attribute, so handlers follow the same contract as always — configuration, not live connections (see IO Handlers). Classes defined inside a function body (tests, notebooks, __main__ scripts) can't be re-imported and are pickled by value instead; both routes are chosen automatically.

items.title: Databricks
items.text: rivers.integrations.databricks runs Databricks jobs as rivers assets. DatabricksResource holds the workspace credentials. Its job_asset method makes an asset that runs a job of the workspace: one asset for the whole job, or one output for each task. A run starts the job, waits until the run ends, and records a materialization.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
pip install rivers[databricks]

DatabricksResource reads its fields from DATABRICKS_* environment variables when you do not give them:

from rivers.integrations.databricks import DatabricksResource

databricks = DatabricksResource()  # DATABRICKS_HOST and DATABRICKS_TOKEN
databricks = DatabricksResource(
    host="https://dbc-1a2b3c4d-5e6f.cloud.databricks.com",
    client_id="...",
    client_secret="...",
)

Give the fields of one authentication method:

Method Fields Environment variables Personal access token token DATABRICKS_TOKEN OAuth for a service principal client_id, client_secret DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID, DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET Azure service principal azure_client_id, azure_client_secret, azure_tenant_id DATABRICKS_AZURE_CLIENT_ID, DATABRICKS_AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET, DATABRICKS_AZURE_TENANT_ID

host is the workspace URL (DATABRICKS_HOST). The fields go to the Databricks SDK. When a field is not set, the SDK uses its own unified authentication: other environment variables (for example ARM_CLIENT_ID, ARM_CLIENT_SECRET and ARM_TENANT_ID, or DATABRICKS_CONFIG_PROFILE), a profile in ~/.databrickscfg, or the Azure or Databricks CLI.

token, client_secret and azure_client_secret are secrets: repr() and the UI's launch dialog do not show them.

Three more fields control how rivers waits for a run:

Field Default Description poll_interval 10 Seconds between status checks of an active run. poll_timeout None Seconds to wait for a run to end. None waits until the run ends. cancel_on_interrupt True Cancel the run when rivers stops waiting before the run ends. See Timeouts and cancel.

items.title: An asset for a job
items.text:
import rivers as rs

daily_sales = databricks.job_asset(123, name="daily_sales")

repo = rs.CodeRepository(
    assets=[daily_sales],
    resources={"databricks": databricks},
)

job_asset does not call Databricks when the code location loads, so you give the asset its name. The asset has the kind databricks. A run starts the job with run_now, waits until the run ends, and records one materialization. A wrong job id fails when the asset runs.

Other keyword arguments go to rs.Asset, for example group, partitions_def, automation_condition, pool, or retry.

job_parameters sets the job's parameters for each run. Give a dict, or a function that gets the asset's context and returns the dict:

from datetime import datetime

daily = rs.PartitionsDefinition.daily(start=datetime(2024, 1, 1))

daily_sales = databricks.job_asset(
    123,
    name="daily_sales",
    partitions_def=daily,
    job_parameters=lambda context: {"date": context.partition_key},
)

items.title: An output for each task
items.text:
sales = databricks.job_asset(456, name="sales", tasks=["orders", "refunds"])

With tasks, the asset is a multi-asset with one output for each task. Each output has the name of its task key. To give an output another name or other settings, map the task key to an rs.AssetDef. An AssetDef without a name gets the task key:

sales = databricks.job_asset(
    456,
    name="sales",
    tasks={
        "ingest_orders": rs.AssetDef("raw/orders"),
        "refunds": rs.AssetDef(group="finance"),
    },
)

A run of all the outputs runs the whole job. A run of some outputs runs only their tasks: rivers puts their task keys in the only field of run_now, and Databricks excludes the other tasks. A task that you do not list runs only when all the outputs run.

When the run ends, each selected task that ended with SUCCESS records a materialization. The other selected outputs fail with DatabricksRunError. When a task that you did not list fails, the outputs do not fail, and the run log has a warning.

rivers does not retry an asset with tasks, because its outputs are recorded one at a time. To retry a task, set max_retries on the task in Databricks.

items.title: The registered resource
items.text:
A run uses the resource registered under the key databricks, not the instance that made the asset. So a run can override the resource's fields, from Python or from the launch dialog in the UI:

repo.materialize(config={"resources": {"databricks": {"poll_timeout": 7200}}})

Without the resource, the code location fails to load with unresolved input 'databricks'.

To register a resource under another key, for example for a second workspace, give the key as resource_key:

staging = DatabricksResource(host="https://dbc-9f8e7d6c-5b4a.cloud.databricks.com", token="...")

repo = rs.CodeRepository(
    assets=[
        databricks.job_asset(123, name="daily_sales"),
        staging.job_asset(123, name="staging_daily_sales", resource_key="databricks_staging"),
    ],
    resources={"databricks": databricks, "databricks_staging": staging},
)

items.title: Waiting and failures
items.text:
While the run is active, rivers gets its state every poll_interval seconds. Each new state of the run is logged with the URL of the run page.

A run must end with SUCCESS. Any other result raises DatabricksRunError, including SUCCESS_WITH_FAILURES, SKIPPED, and INTERNAL_ERROR. The message gives the run's state and the URL of the run page, and the error and stack trace of each task that ended with FAILED, TIMEDOUT, CANCELED, or INTERNAL_ERROR:

Databricks run 4417 ended with FAILED: Task ingest failed with message: Workload failed, see run output for details.
https://dbc-1a2b3c4d-5e6f.cloud.databricks.com/jobs/123/runs/4417
Task ingest FAILED: ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
Traceback (most recent call last): ...

With tasks, the message of a failed output gives the state and the error of the selected tasks that did not succeed.

items.title: Timeouts and cancel
items.text:
Set poll_timeout to stop waiting for long runs:

databricks = DatabricksResource(poll_timeout=3600)

When the run does not end within poll_timeout seconds, rivers raises TimeoutError. A TimeoutError has the failure reason TIMEOUT, so RetryOn.TRANSIENT retries it.

When rivers stops waiting before the run ends, it cancels the run in Databricks. This occurs after poll_timeout, when an API request fails, and on an interrupt such as Ctrl-C. Set cancel_on_interrupt=False to let the run continue in Databricks. A process that is killed, for example a deleted Kubernetes pod, cannot cancel the run.

Canceling a rivers run does not cancel a Databricks run that a step waits for. To limit the run on the Databricks side, set timeout_seconds in the job.

items.title: Metadata
items.text:
The materialization of an asset without tasks has this metadata:

Key Type Description databricks/run_id int The run id. databricks/job_id int The job id. databricks/run_url MetadataValue.url The run page. databricks/duration MetadataValue.duration Seconds from the start of the run to its end, cluster start included. databricks/output/<task key> str The exit value of each notebook task, see below.

The materialization of each output of an asset with tasks has this metadata:

Key Type Description databricks/run_id int The run id of the job. databricks/job_id int The job id. databricks/run_url MetadataValue.url The run page of the task. databricks/duration MetadataValue.duration Seconds from the start of the task to its end. databricks/task_key str The task key. databricks/output str The exit value of the task, when it is a notebook task.

A notebook task can send a value back with dbutils.notebook.exit(). Databricks returns the first 5 MB of each value. Keep values small: they are stored as metadata.

# Last cell of the notebook
dbutils.notebook.exit(json.dumps({"rows": 1200}))

Python script and wheel tasks have no exit value. Their output stays on the run page.

items.title: Compute and retries
items.text:
The step of a job asset only starts the run and waits for it. A Databricks cluster or serverless compute does the work: set it in the job or its tasks. On Kubernetes, compute= sizes the pod of the waiting step, so a small value is enough. It does not change Databricks compute, and neither does retry escalation.

The function of a job asset is async, so its step waits without holding a worker of the executor, and the job assets of one level wait at the same time: all of them with the parallel executor (max_async_concurrent limits them), and up to four with the in-process executor. A waiting step keeps its pool slots until the run ends. To limit how many Databricks runs a backfill starts at the same time, give the assets a pool:

daily_sales = databricks.job_asset(123, name="daily_sales", partitions_def=daily, pool="databricks")

repo = rs.CodeRepository(
    assets=[daily_sales],
    resources={"databricks": databricks},
    pool_limits={"databricks": 4},
)

An asset with tasks takes the pool on each output: rs.AssetDef(pool="databricks").

A rivers retry of an asset without tasks starts a new Databricks run. To retry only Databricks failures:

from rivers.integrations.databricks import DatabricksRunError

daily_sales = databricks.job_asset(
    123,
    name="daily_sales",
    retry=rs.RetryPolicy(max_retries=2, retry_on=[DatabricksRunError]),
)

Databricks can also retry a task itself: set max_retries in the task.

items.title: Run a job in your own asset
items.text:
run_job runs a job of the workspace, and submit_run submits a one-time run of tasks that you give in Python. Both wait as job_asset does, return a DatabricksRun, and raise DatabricksRunError when the run does not succeed. Take the registered resource as a parameter, so that a run's config reaches it too:

import json

@rs.Asset(kinds="databricks")
def customers(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext, databricks: DatabricksResource) -> rs.Materialization:
    run = databricks.submit_run(
        [
            {
                "task_key": "main",
                "notebook_task": {"notebook_path": "/Workspace/etl/customers"},
                "existing_cluster_id": "0101-123456-abcdefgh",
            }
        ],
        run_name="customers",
        log=context.log,
    )
    rows = json.loads(run.outputs["main"])["rows"]
    return rs.Materialization(metadata={"databricks/run_id": run.run_id, "rows": rows})

In an async def asset, use async_run_job and async_submit_run. They take the same arguments and wait without blocking the event loop.

A task is a dict in the form of the Jobs API, or a databricks.sdk.service.jobs.SubmitTask. Other keyword arguments go to WorkspaceClient.jobs.submit, for example run_name, timeout_seconds, git_source, or environments for serverless tasks.

get_client() returns a databricks.sdk.WorkspaceClient for anything else:

@rs.Asset
def warehouses(databricks: DatabricksResource) -> list[str]:
    return [w.name for w in databricks.get_client().warehouses.list()]

See the API reference for all the classes.

items.title: Datadog
items.text: rivers.integrations.datadog sends events and metrics to Datadog. DatadogResource holds the keys and the address of the Agent. Its methods build the hooks and the sensor that post an event when an asset or a run fails, and get_client() returns a client for your own metrics.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
pip install rivers[datadog]

The hooks and the sensor post events to the Datadog API with an API key. They need no Agent. Metrics go to the DogStatsD server of a Datadog Agent; rivers needs no key for them. DatadogResource reads the fields that you do not give from DATADOG_* environment variables, for example DATADOG_API_KEY or DATADOG_API_HOST:

from rivers.integrations.datadog import DatadogResource

datadog = DatadogResource()  # keys from DATADOG_API_KEY and DATADOG_APP_KEY
datadog = DatadogResource(api_key="...", api_host="https://api.datadoghq.eu")  # or explicit
Field Default Description api_key None API key. The hooks and the sensor need it. app_key None Application key, for client.api calls that read data. api_host "https://api.datadoghq.com" The API endpoint of your Datadog site, e.g. "https://api.datadoghq.eu" or "https://api.us5.datadoghq.com". statsd_host DD_AGENT_HOST, else "localhost" DogStatsD host. statsd_port DD_DOGSTATSD_PORT, else 8125 DogStatsD port. statsd_socket_path None DogStatsD Unix socket, e.g. "/var/run/datadog/dsd.socket". Used instead of the host and port. constant_tags [] Tags on every metric and event, e.g. ["env:prod"]. In DATADOG_CONSTANT_TAGS, a JSON list.

On Kubernetes, set these variables in CodeLocation.spec.env: DATADOG_API_KEY from a Secret, and DD_AGENT_HOST from a status.hostIP fieldRef when an Agent runs on each node. Run and step pods get the same variables.

items.title: Alert once per failed run
items.text:
run_failure_sensor returns a run-status sensor that posts one event per failed run of the code location:

import rivers as rs

repo = rs.CodeRepository(
    assets=[orders, revenue],
    sensors=[
        datadog.run_failure_sensor(
            tags=["team:data"],
            ui_location_url="https://rivers.example.com/locations/prod/etl",
            default_status=rs.SensorStatus.Running,
        )
    ],
)

The daemon evaluates the sensor only with default_status=rs.SensorStatus.Running.

The event has the alert type error and the title Run <run id> failed, followed by (job <job>) when the run belongs to a job. Its text lists each failed step with its error, or the launch error:

Run `3f2a…` failed (job `nightly`).

`revenue[2024-01-01]`:
```
ValueError: negative total
```

View run

The event is tagged:

  • run_id:<run id>
  • job:<job> and partition:<partition key>, when the run has them
  • asset:<asset> for each failed step
  • code_location:<name> when RIVERS_CODE_LOCATION_NAME is set. The operator sets it to the name of the CodeLocation on code location and run pods.
  • the sensor's tags, then constant_tags

The run id is also the event's aggregation key, so the events of one run group together. To get notified, create an event monitor that matches these tags, for example asset:revenue.

Parameter Default Description tags None More tags for the event, e.g. ["team:data"]. text_fn built-in (RunStatusSensorContext) -> str. Builds the event text, in Markdown. ui_location_url None The code location's UI URL. When set, the event links to the run at {ui_location_url}/runs/{run_id}. name "datadog_run_failure_sensor" Sensor name. Two Datadog sensors in one repository need distinct names. minimum_interval "30s" Minimum interval between ticks. monitored_jobs None Only report runs of these jobs. None reports every failed run. default_status Stopped Whether the daemon evaluates the sensor.

Each tick posts for at most 5 runs; later failures go out on the next ticks. When Datadog rejects an event or cannot be reached within 10 s, the tick fails with the error, and the sensor does not try that run again. See how runs are picked.

items.title: Alert per asset
items.text:
failure_hook and success_hook return hooks that post an event when an asset step fails or succeeds:

@rs.Asset(hooks=[datadog.failure_hook(tags=["team:finance"])])
def orders() -> int: ...

@rs.Asset(hooks=[datadog.success_hook(text_fn=lambda c: f"`{c.asset_name}` is fresh")])
def revenue() -> int: ...

The event has the title Asset <asset> failed and the alert type error, or Asset <asset> succeeded and success. The default text names the asset and the run, and quotes the error on failure. The event is tagged asset:<asset> and run_id:<run id>, then code_location:<name> as above, the hook's tags, and constant_tags. The hook context has no partition key, so the event has no partition tag; the run-failure sensor's event has one.

Parameter Default Description tags None More tags for the event. text_fn built-in (HookContext) -> str. Builds the event text, in Markdown. ui_location_url None The code location's UI URL. When set, the event links to the run. name "datadog_failure_hook" / "datadog_success_hook" Hook name.

A hook fires once per step, so a run with three failed assets posts three events. Use run_failure_sensor for one event per run. A Datadog error in a hook is logged and does not fail the step.

Without an API key, failure_hook, success_hook, and run_failure_sensor raise ValueError when you build them, not when the first event is due.

items.title: Send metrics from your own code
items.text:
Register DatadogResource as a resource to send metrics or events from assets and sensors:

import pyarrow as pa

@rs.Asset
def orders(datadog: DatadogResource) -> pa.Table:
    table = load_orders()
    datadog.get_client().gauge("orders.rows", table.num_rows, tags=["asset:orders"])
    return table

repo = rs.CodeRepository(assets=[orders], resources={"datadog": DatadogResource()})

get_client() returns a DatadogClient, a datadog.DogStatsd client with constant_tags on every metric. Resources with the same DogStatsD fields share one client per process. Its methods send through the Agent: gauge, increment, decrement, histogram, distribution, set, timing, timed, event, and service_check.

Each distinct set of tags on a metric is a separate custom metric in Datadog. Do not tag metrics with run ids or partition keys.

client.api is datadogpy's HTTP API client, for example client.api.Event.create(...) or client.api.Monitor.get_all(). datadogpy keeps its keys for the whole process: get_client() sets them to the resource's api_key, app_key, and api_host. It returns a rejected request as a dict with an errors key; it does not raise.

items.title: Traces through OpenTelemetry
items.text:
rivers itself exports traces over OTLP/gRPC when OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT is set (see Observability). This needs no rivers[datadog]. The Datadog Agent accepts OTLP from version 7.32: enable its OTLP receiver, for example with DD_OTLP_CONFIG_RECEIVER_PROTOCOLS_GRPC_ENDPOINT=0.0.0.0:4317, and point OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT at it. The spans then show in Datadog APM under the service rivers, or the name in OTEL_SERVICE_NAME. On Kubernetes, OpenTelemetry export shows how to point the pods at an Agent on the same node.

The two work together. Traces show what rivers did and how long it took; this integration tells Datadog when an asset or a run fails, and carries the metrics that your assets send.

items.title: dataframely
items.text: rivers.integrations.dataframely validates asset outputs against dataframely schemas. Give an asset a dataframely return hint, and rivers checks each polars frame that the asset returns.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
pip install rivers[dataframely]

You do not import the integration: rivers finds it from the return hint.

items.title: Validate an asset's output
items.text:
Annotate the return with dy.DataFrame[Schema]:

import dataframely as dy
import polars as pl

import rivers as rs

class Orders(dy.Schema):
    """Orders placed in the shop."""

    id = dy.Int64(primary_key=True, min=0, description="Order id")
    amount = dy.Float64(nullable=True, min_exclusive=0)
    status = dy.String(regex="^(open|closed)$")

    @dy.rule()
    def open_orders_have_amount(cls) -> pl.Expr:
        return (pl.col("status") != "open") | pl.col("amount").is_not_null()

@rs.Asset
def orders() -> dy.DataFrame[Orders]:
    return pl.read_parquet("orders.parquet")

When the asset returns, rivers calls Orders.validate(frame). A valid frame is stored and recorded. An invalid frame fails the step with AssetOutputValidationError, and nothing is stored. Downstream assets do not run.

These return hints hold a schema:

Return hint Value dy.DataFrame[Schema] polars.DataFrame dy.LazyFrame[Schema] polars.LazyFrame Annotated[pl.DataFrame, Schema], Annotated[pl.LazyFrame, Schema] The frame, checked against Schema dy.DataFrame[Schema] \| None A frame, or None (not validated)

A value of the wrong type, for example a dict for dy.DataFrame[Orders], fails like any other return type check.

items.title: Lazy frames
items.text:
@rs.Asset
def open_orders(orders: pl.DataFrame) -> dy.LazyFrame[Orders]:
    return orders.lazy().filter(pl.col("status") == "open")

When the asset returns a LazyFrame, rivers checks its columns and their types, and does not collect the frame. dataframely adds its row checks to the frame, and runs them when the frame is collected:

  • DeltaIOHandler and DuckDBIOHandler collect the frame when they write it. A bad row fails the asset's step with the write's error, which holds dataframely's report, and the table does not change.
  • PickleIOHandler stores the frame without collecting it, so a bad row fails the step that reads and collects it.

items.title: Casting
items.text:
dataframely checks types strictly: a column with the wrong type fails the step. To cast the columns to the schema's types first, set cast in the schema's Config:

class Prices(dy.Schema):
    price = dy.Float64()

    class Config:
        cast = True

@rs.Asset
def prices() -> dy.DataFrame[Prices]:
    return pl.DataFrame({"price": [1, 2]})  # stored with price as Float64

rivers then calls Prices.validate(frame, cast=True). Only rivers reads Config. A direct call to Prices.validate(frame) does not cast.

items.title: The stored frame
items.text: rivers stores the frame that dataframely returns, not the frame that the asset returned. Columns that the schema does not define are dropped. With Config.cast, the columns have the schema's types.

items.title: Schema metadata
items.text:
Each validated materialization records the schema as dataframely/schema, a JSON MetadataValue. The UI shows it with the other metadata of the materialization:

{
  "name": "Orders",
  "description": "Orders placed in the shop.",
  "columns": [
    {"name": "id", "type": "Int64", "nullable": false, "primary_key": true, "unique": false, "description": "Order id", "checks": ["min=0"]},
    {"name": "amount", "type": "Float64", "nullable": true, "primary_key": false, "unique": false, "description": null, "checks": ["min_exclusive=0", "inf", "nan"]},
    {"name": "status", "type": "String", "nullable": false, "primary_key": false, "unique": false, "description": null, "checks": ["regex='^(open|closed)$'"]}
  ],
  "checks": ["open_orders_have_amount"]
}

A check has the name that dataframely's failure report uses, with its bound if it has one. A dataframely/schema entry that the asset sets itself, with context.add_output_metadata() or Output(metadata=...), replaces this one.

items.title: Failures
items.text:
The message has dataframely's report: each rule that failed, and the number of rows that failed it.

AssetOutputValidationError: Asset 'orders' returned a value that does not match 'dataframely._typing.DataFrame[pipeline.Orders]': 4 rules failed validation:
 - 'open_orders_have_amount' failed for 1 rows
 * Column 'id' failed validation for 1 rules:
   - 'min' failed for 1 rows
 * Column 'amount' failed validation for 1 rules:
   - 'min_exclusive' failed for 1 rows
 * Column 'status' failed validation for 1 rules:
   - 'regex' failed for 1 rows

A missing column, or a column with the wrong type, fails with dataframely's SchemaError text instead.

Both executors validate the same way. The parallel executor validates a sync step in its worker process.

items.title: Multi-asset outputs
items.text:
A multi-asset has one return hint for all its outputs. Give an output its own hint with AssetDef(type_hint=...). rivers validates that output's frame the same way as a returned frame:

@rs.Asset.from_multi(
    output_defs=[
        rs.AssetDef("orders", type_hint=dy.DataFrame[Orders]),
        rs.AssetDef("refunds"),
    ]
)
def load():
    yield rs.Output(read_orders(), output_name="orders")
    yield rs.Output(read_refunds(), output_name="refunds")

An invalid frame fails its output. See Return type checks for the other outputs.

items.title: Inputs
items.text: rivers validates return values, not inputs: a frame is validated once, when its asset writes it. Annotate a downstream parameter with the frame type, for example orders: pl.DataFrame. DeltaIOHandler and DuckDBIOHandler read by that type and do not accept a dataframely hint there.

items.title: dbt
items.text:
rivers.integrations.dbt makes the models, seeds, and snapshots of a dbt project into rivers assets, and runs dbt to build them:

  • DbtProject reads the project's manifest and defines the assets.
  • DbtResource runs dbt commands and reports each output that dbt builds.
  • DbtNode is one model, seed, snapshot, or source of the manifest. The functions that change the outputs get it.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
pip install rivers[dbt] dbt-duckdb   # dbt-core, and the adapter for your warehouse

rivers supports dbt-core 1.7.10 and later 1.x releases.

items.title: Define the assets
items.text:
from pathlib import Path

import rivers as rs
from rivers.integrations.dbt import DbtProject, DbtResource

project = DbtProject(Path(__file__).parent / "analytics")

@project.assets()
def analytics(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext, dbt: DbtResource):
    yield from dbt.cli(["build"], context)

repo = rs.CodeRepository(
    assets=[analytics],
    resources={"dbt": DbtResource(project_dir=project)},
)

project.assets() returns a decorator that builds one multi-asset. Each model, seed, and snapshot is an output. By default, node.output_def() builds it:

Setting Value Name The resource name, e.g. orders. Version 2 of a versioned model is orders_v2. Code version The checksum dbt records for the resource's file. When the file changes, the asset is stale. Group The resource's dbt group. Tags The resource's dbt tags. Kinds dbt. Metadata dbt/unique_id, dbt/relation, dbt/materialized, and dbt/description.

rivers then adds to each output:

  • Deps: the resources that it refs, as lineage-only deps. An ephemeral model builds no table, so the deps go through it to the resources it reads.
  • With dbt-duckdb, the duckdb/schema and duckdb/table metadata.

Tests, sources, and ephemeral models are not assets.

Other keyword arguments go to rs.Asset.from_multi, e.g. name, group (for resources without a dbt group), partitions_def, hooks, retry, or automation_condition.

items.title: Write the manifest
items.text:
DbtProject reads manifest.json from the target directory. Write it before the code location loads, e.g. when you build its image:

dbt parse --project-dir analytics --profiles-dir analytics

project.prepare() does the same: it runs dbt parse and replaces the manifest in one step. During development, call it in the module, so that a reload picks up your dbt changes:

project = DbtProject(Path(__file__).parent / "analytics")
project.prepare()

prepare() uses the profile, like other dbt commands. A selection also uses it when the definitions load. When the project uses packages, run dbt deps first. Parse with the target that the runs use: the manifest records the database and schema of each table, which go into dbt/relation, so use a placeholder only for a secret.

DbtProject field Default Description project_dir required The directory with dbt_project.yml. target_path "target" The directory with manifest.json, relative to project_dir. profiles_dir None The directory with profiles.yml, for prepare(), selections, and a DbtResource made from the project. None uses dbt's search. profile None The profile to use instead of the project's. target None The target to use instead of the profile's default. asset_def_fn None Builds the output of each model, seed, and snapshot. None uses DbtNode.output_def. See Change the outputs. source_asset_fn None Names the rivers asset that loads a dbt source. None adds no dep for sources. See Sources.

items.title: Run dbt
items.text:
The body runs dbt with dbt.cli(args, context), and yield from reports each output when dbt finishes it:

  • dbt builds the outputs that the run selected. A run of every output uses the definition's selection. A run of some outputs selects each one by its fqn and keeps the definition's exclude: repo.materialize(["customers"]) runs dbt build --select fqn:analytics.marts.customers.
  • dbt's log goes to the run log.
  • When dbt fails, the outputs that it built keep their materializations. The other outputs fail with dbt's error, which names each failed or skipped resource.

The body must take the resource as a parameter, as in the example: a body that makes its own DbtResource instead raises TypeError.

Each materialization records:

Key Type Description dbt/invocation_id text dbt's id for the command. dbt/execution_time duration How long dbt took to build the resource. dbt/message text The adapter's message, e.g. INSERT 3. dbt/rows_affected int Rows the adapter reports, if it does. dbt/tests JSON The status of each test on the output, e.g. {"unique_orders_id": "pass"}.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
rivers has no asset checks. In a dbt build, dbt tests each resource after it builds it, and skips the resources downstream of a failed test. rivers follows dbt:

  • An output with tests is reported when its tests finish. dbt/tests lists their status.
  • A failed test with severity error fails the output that it tests, with the test's message. dbt skips the downstream resources, so they fail too. dbt has already rebuilt the table of the tested output.
  • A test with severity warn does not fail the output. Its status is warn.
  • A generic test belongs to the model it is defined on. A singular test belongs to each model that it refs.
  • A failed source test or unit test fails the run. Its message is in the error.

dbt run runs no tests: each output is reported when dbt builds it.

items.title: DbtResource
items.text:
Field Default Description project_dir required The directory with dbt_project.yml, or a DbtProject. profiles_dir None The directory with profiles.yml. None uses dbt's search: the project directory, then ~/.dbt. profile None The profile to use instead of the project's. target None The target to use instead of the profile's default. executable None The dbt executable, e.g. "dbt" or a path. None runs the dbt-core installed with rivers.

Give the resource the DbtProject, as in the example. It then takes the project's profiles_dir, profile, and target, so dbt runs with the settings that prepare() and the selections use. Each field takes the first value that it finds:

  1. The value that you give the resource.
  2. The project's value, if it is not None.
