  3. The environment variable that dbt reads: DBT_PROJECT_DIR, DBT_PROFILES_DIR, DBT_PROFILE, or DBT_TARGET.
  4. The default.

Each command runs in a new process with its own target directory, so commands can run at the same time. The directory is removed when the command ends. The command starts from the project's partial_parse.msgpack, so dbt parses only the files that changed. For prepare(), selections, and the commands in a project.assets() body, the file is in the project's target_path. Elsewhere, it is in target in the project directory, or in DBT_TARGET_PATH when you set it. rivers sets DBT_SEND_ANONYMOUS_USAGE_STATS=false unless you set it.

rivers reads dbt's JSON debug log. Do not pass --log-format, --log-level, or --quiet.

items.title: Other commands
items.text:
Without a context, cli runs the command as given and yields nothing. wait() runs it to the end and raises DbtError when dbt fails:

@rs.Asset(deps=[rs.AssetDef.dep("orders")])
def export_orders(dbt: DbtResource) -> None:
    dbt.cli(["run-operation", "export_orders"]).wait()

Pass target_path to keep run_results.json and the other artifacts. In a project.assets() body, your own --select, --exclude, or --selector replaces the selection of the run.

items.title: Async
items.text:
The body can be an async generator. async for yields the same materializations as yield from, and dbt's errors fail the outputs in the same way:

@project.assets()
async def analytics(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext, dbt: DbtResource):
    async for materialization in dbt.cli(["build"], context):
        yield materialization

dbt runs in its own process, so the step only waits for dbt. An async body waits on an event loop, so its step does not hold a worker of the executor:

  • With the parallel executor, a sync body holds a worker process until dbt ends. An async body leaves the workers to the other steps, and all the async steps of a level wait at the same time. max_async_concurrent limits them.
  • With the in-process executor, the sync steps of a level run one after the other. Up to four async steps of a level wait at the same time.

A waiting step keeps its pool slots until dbt ends.

In an async def asset, await dbt.cli([...]).async_wait() runs a command without blocking the event loop. It raises DbtError as wait() does:

@rs.Asset(deps=[rs.AssetDef.dep("orders")])
async def export_orders(dbt: DbtResource) -> None:
    await dbt.cli(["run-operation", "export_orders"]).async_wait()

When rivers cancels an async step, e.g. on Ctrl-C, dbt stops as it does for a sync body. It gets an interrupt, so that it cancels its queries, and rivers kills it when it still runs 25 seconds later. On Windows, rivers ends dbt at once.

items.title: Select resources
items.text:
select, exclude, and selector take dbt's node selection syntax. Use them to split a project into definitions, e.g. to partition the incremental models:

@project.assets(select="config.materialized:incremental", partitions_def=daily, name="incremental")
def incremental(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext, dbt: DbtResource): ...

@project.assets(exclude="config.materialized:incremental", name="analytics")
def analytics(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext, dbt: DbtResource): ...

A selection other than the default runs dbt ls when the definitions load. dbt ls needs what dbt parse needs, e.g. profiles.yml and each env var that the profile or the project reads. dbt does not connect to the warehouse, so a placeholder for a secret, such as a password, is enough.

rivers caches the result in the target directory. The load runs dbt ls again for a new selection or a new manifest: each dbt parse or prepare() writes a new manifest, also when no file changed. To put the cache in the image, load the definitions once when you build it, after dbt parse:

dbt parse --project-dir analytics --profiles-dir analytics
python -c "import my_module"   # the code location's module

The code location then loads without dbt ls, so the load does not need the profile.

A dep on a resource outside the selection refers to that resource's output by name. Names are project-wide: the project's asset_def_fn builds the output of every model, seed, and snapshot, also of the ones that a definition does not select. So a dep has the same name in every definition. Define every resource that the selected resources ref, e.g. with a second definition as above: a dep on an asset that no definition builds fails the repository's validation.

items.title: Sources
items.text:
A dbt source adds no dep by default. To make the models that read a source run after the rivers asset that loads it, give the project a source_asset_fn. It gets each source that a selected output reads, also through ephemeral models, and returns the name of the asset that loads the source, or None for no dep:

project = DbtProject(
    Path(__file__).parent / "analytics",
    source_asset_fn=lambda source: f"{source.props['source_name']}_{source.name}",  # e.g. raw_payments
)

The asset must be in the repository.

items.title: Partitions
items.text:
Give dbt the partition as vars, and filter on them in the model:

import json
from datetime import datetime

daily = rs.PartitionsDefinition.daily(start=datetime(2024, 1, 1))

@project.assets(select="config.materialized:incremental", partitions_def=daily)
def incremental(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext, dbt: DbtResource):
    start, end = context.partition_time_window
    dbt_vars = {"min_date": start.isoformat(), "max_date": end.isoformat()}
    yield from dbt.cli(["build", "--vars", json.dumps(dbt_vars)], context)

{{ config(materialized='incremental', incremental_strategy='delete+insert', unique_key='order_date') }}

select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
where order_date >= '{{ var("min_date") }}' and order_date < '{{ var("max_date") }}'

With delete+insert, a second run of a partition replaces its rows.

items.title: Read the tables downstream
items.text:
A downstream asset can depend on a model with rs.AssetDef.dep("customers") and query the table. Or give the definition an io_handler that reads tables. With dbt-duckdb, each output has duckdb/schema and duckdb/table metadata, so DuckDBIOHandler loads it:

import pyarrow as pa
from rivers.integrations.duckdb import DuckDBIOHandler, DuckDBResource

warehouse = DuckDBResource(database="warehouse.duckdb")  # the path in profiles.yml

@project.assets(io_handler=DuckDBIOHandler(resource=warehouse))
def analytics(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext, dbt: DbtResource):
    yield from dbt.cli(["build"], context)

@rs.Asset
def customer_count(customers: pa.Table) -> int:
    return customers.num_rows

The handler only reads: dbt writes the tables.

items.title: Change the outputs
items.text:
The project's asset_def_fn builds the output of each model, seed, and snapshot. It takes a DbtNode and returns an AssetDef. node.output_def(...) returns the default output with the fields that you give:

from rivers.integrations.dbt import DbtNode

def asset_def(node: DbtNode) -> rs.AssetDef:
    return node.output_def(
        name=f"analytics_{node.asset_name}",
        group="raw" if node.resource_type == "seed" else "analytics",
    )

project = DbtProject(Path(__file__).parent / "analytics", asset_def_fn=asset_def)
DbtNode Description unique_id dbt's id, e.g. model.analytics.orders. name The resource name, e.g. orders. resource_type model, seed, snapshot, or source. props The resource's entry in manifest.json, e.g. node.props["config"], node.props["meta"], or node.props["source_name"]. asset_name The default name: name, with _v<version> for a versioned model.

metadata= replaces the default metadata. To keep the dbt/ keys, add to them: node.output_def(metadata=node.output_def().metadata | {"team": "finance"}).

rivers adds the deps and the duckdb/ keys to the output that the function returns. The deps and the duckdb/ keys that the function returns stay, e.g. deps=[rs.AssetDef.dep("crm_export")].

The function runs for every model, seed, and snapshot of the project, so a dep on a resource of another definition gets the same name. An output without a name raises ValueError, and so do two resources with the same output name.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• A run of some outputs lists each one in --select. On Windows, the command line can be too long for a run of more than about 1,000 models.
  • dbt-core 2, the dbt Fusion engine, is not supported.
  • A microbatch model with a partial success fails its output.

items.title: Delta Lake
items.text: The DeltaIOHandler persists asset outputs as Delta Lake tables. It supports PyArrow, Polars, pandas, and DataFusion data types, partitioned writes, and full MERGE INTO operations.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
pip install rivers[delta]

# Plus at least one of:
pip install rivers[pyarrow]
pip install rivers[polars]
pip install rivers[pandas]
pip install rivers[datafusion]
pip install rivers[duckdb]
pip install rivers[pyspark]

items.title: Basic usage
items.text:
import polars as pl
import rivers as rs
from rivers.io_handlers.delta import DeltaIOHandler

io = DeltaIOHandler(table_uri="/data/delta")

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io)
def users() -> pl.DataFrame:
    return pl.DataFrame({
        "id": [1, 2, 3],
        "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"],
    })

items.title: Usage with Spark
items.text:
import pandas as pd
from pyspark.sql.dataframe import DataFrame as SparkDataFrame
import rivers as rs
from rivers.io_handlers.delta import DeltaIOHandler

spark_session = ... # your spark session initialization
io = DeltaIOHandler(
    table_uri="/data/delta",
    handler_config={"spark_session": spark_session}
)

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io)
def users() -> SparkDataFrame:
    return spark.createDataFrame(
        pd.DataFrame({
            "id": [1, 2, 3],
            "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"],
        })
    )

In above cases, the handler creates a Delta table at /data/delta/users/.

items.title: Supported types
Read with DuckDB
items.text:
A duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation input reads the table with DuckDB's delta_scan. The relation is lazy. delta/columns, the partition predicate, and file statistics prune the files that DuckDB reads, and delta/version reads an older version. A relation output streams into delta-rs, which writes the table.

import duckdb
import rivers as rs

@rs.Asset
def summary(orders: duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation, users: duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation) -> duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation:
    return orders.join(users, "user_id").aggregate("country, sum(amount) AS total")

Inputs that one step reads share one DuckDB connection per thread, so the step can join them. To set extensions, secrets, or settings, pass a DuckDBResource:

from rivers.integrations.duckdb import DuckDBResource

io = DeltaIOHandler(
    table_uri="s3://bucket/delta",
    storage_options={"AWS_REGION": "eu-west-1"},
    handler_config={"duckdb": DuckDBResource(connection_config={"threads": 8})},
)

The handler turns storage_options into a DuckDB secret for the table's bucket or container:

  • S3: the access key, secret, session token, region, and endpoint. Without a key, DuckDB uses the AWS credential chain.
  • Azure: an account key, a SAS token, or a service principal. Without one, DuckDB uses the Azure credential chain.
  • GCS: not supported. DuckDB reads GCS only with HMAC keys; set them with DuckDBResource(secrets=...).

items.title: Write modes
items.text:
Set the default mode on the handler, or override per-asset via metadata:

# Handler-level default
io = DeltaIOHandler(table_uri="/data/delta", mode="append")

# Per-asset override
@rs.Asset(io_handler=io, metadata={"delta/mode": "overwrite"})
def events() -> pl.DataFrame:
    ...

items.title: Arrow type handlers
items.text: Mode Behavior overwrite Replace the table (or partition) append Add rows to existing table error Fail if table exists ignore Skip write if table exists merge MERGE INTO (see below) create_or_replace Drop and recreate schema, then append

items.title: Supported table write modes
items.text: Mode Behavior overwrite Replace the table (or partition) append Add rows to existing table error Fail if table exists ignore Skip write if table exists

items.title: Support schema modes
items.text: Mode Behavior overwrite Replace the table (or partition) merge MERGE INTO (see below)

items.title: Partitioned writes
items.text:
Combine with PartitionsDefinition and partition_expr:

@rs.Asset(
    io_handler=io,
    partitions_def=rs.PartitionsDefinition.daily(start=datetime(2024, 1, 1)),
    metadata={"delta/partition_expr": "date"},
)
def daily_events() -> pl.DataFrame:
    ...

When writing in overwrite mode with a partition key, the handler generates a predicate to overwrite only the target partition.

items.title: Merge operations
items.text:
For upserts, deduplication, and other MERGE INTO patterns:

from rivers.io_handlers.delta import DeltaIOHandler, MergeConfig

io = DeltaIOHandler(
    table_uri="/data/delta",
    mode="merge",
    merge_config=MergeConfig(
        merge_type="upsert",
        predicate="s.id = t.id",
    ),
)

items.title: Merge types
items.text: Type Behavior upsert Update matched rows, insert unmatched deduplicate_insert Insert only unmatched rows update_only Update matched rows only replace_delete_unmatched Update matched, delete unmatched in target custom Full control via MergeOperationsConfig

items.title: Custom merge operations
items.text:
from rivers.io_handlers.delta import (
    MergeConfig,
    MergeOperationsConfig,
    WhenMatchedUpdateAll,
    WhenNotMatchedInsertAll,
)

io = DeltaIOHandler(
    table_uri="/data/delta",
    mode="merge",
    merge_config=MergeConfig(
        merge_type="custom",
        predicate="s.id = t.id",
        operations=MergeOperationsConfig(
            when_matched_update_all=[
                WhenMatchedUpdateAll(predicate="s.updated_at > t.updated_at"),
            ],
            when_not_matched_insert_all=[
                WhenNotMatchedInsertAll(),
            ],
        ),
    ),
)

items.title: Storage options
items.text:
Pass storage credentials for remote backends:

io = DeltaIOHandler(
    table_uri="s3://my-bucket/delta",
    storage_options={
        "aws_region": "us-east-1",
        "aws_access_key_id": "...",
        "aws_secret_access_key": "...",
    },
)

items.title: Handler configuration
items.text: Handler configuration allows you to pass custom handler properties like a SparkSession object when using a Spark type handler.

items.title: Example reading my_table in a cloud blob storage with Spark
items.text:
spark_session = ... # your spark session initialized with cloud credentials
io_spark = DeltaIOHandler(
    table_uri="/cloud/path/to/my_table",
    handler_config={"spark_session": spark_session}
)
ctx = rs.InputContext(
    asset_name="tbl",
    downstream_asset="consumer",
    type_hint=pyspark.sql.DataFrame,
)
spark_df = handler.load_input(ctx)

items.title: Table configuration
items.text:
Set Delta table properties:

io = DeltaIOHandler(
    table_uri="/data/delta",
    table_config={
        "delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration": "interval 30 days",
    },
)

Override per-asset via metadata:

@rs.Asset(
    io_handler=io,
    metadata={
        "delta/table_configuration": '{"delta.enableChangeDataFeed": "true"}',
    },
)
def events() -> pl.DataFrame:
    ...

items.title: Reading data
items.text:
Downstream assets read data by type annotation:

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io)
def summary(users: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return users.group_by("region").len()

items.title: Column selection
items.text:
Load only specific columns:

@rs.Asset(
    io_handler=io,
    metadata={"delta/columns": '["id", "name"]'},
)
def user_names(users: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    ...

items.title: Time travel
items.text:
Read a specific table version:

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io, metadata={"delta/version": "3"})
def historical(users: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    ...

items.title: Maintenance actions
items.text:
Subclass DeltaAsset and the standard maintenance verbs come built in — optimize, vacuum, and delete, resolved against the asset's DeltaIOHandler (same URI, same credentials, same commit configuration the write path uses):

from rivers.io_handlers.delta import DeltaAsset  # also exported as rs.DeltaAsset

class Orders(DeltaAsset):
    io_handler = WAREHOUSE

    @classmethod
    def materialize(cls) -> pl.DataFrame:
        return pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3]})


repo = rs.CodeRepository(assets=[Orders])
repo.run_action("optimize")
repo.run_action("optimize", partition_key=pk)  # only that partition's files
repo.run_action("vacuum", config={"orders": {"retention_hours": 24}})
repo.run_action("delete", partition_key=pk)
Verb Declaration Behavior optimize Unchanged + Exclusive + Optional key Compacts small files; z-orders instead when z_order_by is configured. With a key, only that partition's files; without one, the whole table. From the UI or gRPC, the keyless form needs an explicit whole-asset choice. vacuum Unchanged + Exclusive + Keyless Removes unreferenced files; retention_hours and enforce_retention_duration via config. Table-wide — runs without a partition key, on partitioned assets too. delete Unmaterialize + Exclusive + DownstreamFirst + Optional key Deletes the keyed partition's rows via partition_predicate, or every row without a key — both forms valid on partitioned assets. From the UI or gRPC, the keyless form needs an explicit whole-asset choice.

On a table that does not exist yet, optimize and vacuum report unchanged instead of failing, so a fleet-wide repo.run_action("optimize") skips never-materialized assets; delete still applies Unmaterialize, so dangling state clears even when the physical table is already gone. DeltaAsset sets kinds = "delta" and defines no materialize(), so it is a mixin — subclasses supply it, and a subclass redefining a verb replaces it.

items.title: Custom verbs
items.text:
For verbs beyond the built-ins, DeltaIOHandler exposes the same per-asset resolution the write path uses, so custom asset actions stay symmetric with writes:

class Events(DeltaAsset):
    io_handler = WAREHOUSE

    @classmethod
    def materialize(cls) -> pl.DataFrame: ...

    @rs.action(outcome=rs.Outcome.MayMaterialize)
    @classmethod
    def merge_late(cls, ctx: rs.ActionContext) -> rs.ActionResult:
        h = ctx.io_handler
        late = fetch_late_rows(ctx.partition_key)
        if late.is_empty():
            return rs.ActionResult.unchanged()
        merge_into(
            h.asset_table_uri(ctx.asset_name, ctx.asset_metadata),
            late,
            storage_options=h.storage_options,
        )
        return rs.ActionResult.materialized(metadata={"rows_merged": len(late)})
  • asset_table_uri(asset_name, asset_metadata) — {table_uri}/{leaf}, honoring the delta/root_name override.
  • partition_predicate(asset_metadata, ctx.partition) — the SQL predicate for the partition(s) being acted on, honoring delta/partition_expr.
  • partition_filters(asset_metadata, ctx.partition) — the same partitions as delta-rs partition_filters, one conjunction per key, for optimize.

Because optimize declares Exclusive, a keyless run claims the asset's implicit pool for the whole asset: it never overlaps a materialize of the same asset, and contention shows up in the UI as StepSlotWaiting. A keyed optimize or delete claims only its partition. Materialize steps never exclude each other, so declaring an exclusive action does not serialize ordinary runs.

items.title: dlt
items.text:
rivers.integrations.dlt loads dlt sources as rivers assets. Each resource of a source becomes one output of a multi-asset:

  • DltSourceAssets reads a dlt source and gives each resource an output.
  • Its load method runs a dlt pipeline on the source.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
pip install rivers[dlt]

Also install the dlt extra for your destination, e.g. pip install "dlt[snowflake]".

items.title: Assets from a source
items.text:
import dlt
import rivers as rs
from rivers.integrations.dlt import DltSourceAssets


@dlt.source(name="github")
def github_source(repo: str = "dlt-hub/dlt"):
    @dlt.resource(primary_key="id", write_disposition="merge")
    def issues(): ...

    @dlt.resource(primary_key="id", write_disposition="merge")
    def pull_requests(): ...

    return issues, pull_requests


github = DltSourceAssets(github_source())


@github.assets(name="github", group="github")
def github_assets(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext):
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline("github", destination="snowflake", dataset_name="github")
    yield from github.load(context, pipeline)


repo = rs.CodeRepository(assets=[github_assets])

This defines the assets github_issues and github_pull_requests, materialized together by the step github. github.assets(...) builds the multi-asset; its keyword arguments go to Asset.from_multi, e.g. name, group, partitions_def, io_handler, hooks, or retry. The function makes the dlt pipeline and loads the source: github.load yields one materialization per resource.

DltSourceAssets takes the dlt source, e.g. github_source(). Use github_source().with_resources("issues") for some of its resources.

The function runs in the process that runs the step, and a dlt source cannot be sent to another process. With the parallel executor, define the DltSourceAssets and the function at module level in an importable module: the worker imports them.

items.title: Asset names
items.text: An output is named after the source and the resource: <source>_<resource>, e.g. github_issues. Use an asset_def_fn to choose other names. Two resources with the same output name raise ValueError.

items.title: Run part of a source
items.text:
Materialize some of the outputs, and the pipeline loads only their resources:

repo.materialize(selection=["github_issues"])

A dlt transformer still reads from its parent resource, but the parent's table does not load.

items.title: The pipeline and the source
items.text:
The function makes the pipeline in each run, so it can use resources and config like any asset. For example, keep the destination's password in a resource:

from pydantic import SecretStr


class Warehouse(rs.Resource):
    host: str
    password: SecretStr

    def pipeline(self, name: str) -> dlt.Pipeline:
        credentials = f"postgresql://loader:{self.password.get_secret_value()}@{self.host}/analytics"
        destination = dlt.destinations.postgres(credentials=credentials)
        return dlt.pipeline(name, destination=destination, dataset_name=name)


@github.assets(name="github")
def github_assets(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext, warehouse: Warehouse):
    yield from github.load(context, warehouse.pipeline("github"))

load loads the source of DltSourceAssets in every run. To build the source in the run, for example from the partition, give it to load: github.load(context, pipeline, github_source(repo=...)). It must have the resources of the selected outputs. A resource made from a generator object, as in dlt.resource(rows()), runs only once: give such a source to load in each run.

items.title: What a run records
items.text:
dlt's load summary goes to the step log. Each materialization has this metadata:

Key Type Description dlt/load_id str The load package of the run, as in the _dlt_load_id column. Not set when the run extracted nothing. dlt/dataset str The dataset that the tables are in. dlt/rows_loaded int Rows loaded into the resource's table in this run, without its nested tables. dlt/row_counts MetadataValue.json Rows loaded per table, with the nested tables, e.g. {"issues": 30, "issues__labels": 41}. dlt/columns MetadataValue.json The columns and dlt data types of each table.

A resource that raises, or a failed normalize step, fails every selected output: dlt extracts a source into one load package, and loads nothing when the extract fails.

A load job that fails fails every selected output, with dlt's default load.raise_on_failed_jobs = true. With false, dlt finishes the package. rivers then records the resources whose tables loaded, and the step fails for the others with DestinationHasFailedJobs.

Before each run, the pipeline aborts the load packages that a failed run left (pipeline.abort_packages()). dlt rewinds the pipeline state, such as incremental cursors, to before those packages, so the run extracts their data again.

To try a failed load again, give the assets a retry policy:

from dlt.common.destination.exceptions import DestinationHasFailedJobs
from dlt.pipeline.exceptions import PipelineStepFailed


@github.assets(
    name="github",
    retry=rs.RetryPolicy(max_retries=2, retry_on=[PipelineStepFailed, DestinationHasFailedJobs]),
)
def github_assets(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext): ...

items.title: Partitions
items.text:
Build the source from the partition, and give it to load:

from datetime import datetime

from rivers.integrations.dlt import output_def


@dlt.source(name="events")
def events_source(since: datetime | None = None, until: datetime | None = None):
    @dlt.resource
    def page_views():
        yield from read_page_views(since, until)

    return page_views


events = DltSourceAssets(
    events_source(),
    asset_def_fn=lambda resource: output_def(resource, pool="events_pipeline"),
)


@events.assets(
    name="events",
    partitions_def=rs.PartitionsDefinition.daily(start=datetime(2024, 1, 1)),
)
def events_assets(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext):
    since, until = context.partition_time_window
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline("events", destination="snowflake", dataset_name="events")
    yield from events.load(context, pipeline, events_source(since=since, until=until))


repo = rs.CodeRepository(assets=[events_assets], pool_limits={"events_pipeline": 1})

A dlt pipeline keeps its state and load packages in one working directory, so two runs of one pipeline must not overlap. Give the outputs a pool with a limit of 1, as above, or give each concurrent run its own pipeline name.

For an incremental resource, pass the window as initial_value and end_value of dlt.sources.incremental. With an end_value, dlt loads that range and does not change the incremental state.

items.title: Change the outputs
items.text:
asset_def_fn builds the output of each resource. It takes the dlt resource and returns an AssetDef. output_def(resource, ...) returns the default output with the fields that you give:

from rivers.integrations.dlt import output_def


def asset_def(resource) -> rs.AssetDef:
    return output_def(
        resource,
        name=f"raw_{resource.name}",
        kinds=["dlt", "snowflake"],
        deps=[rs.AssetDef.dep("github_app")] if resource.name == "issues" else [],
    )


github = DltSourceAssets(github_source(), asset_def_fn=asset_def)
Field Default name <source>_<resource>, e.g. github_issues. kinds ["dlt"]. metadata dlt/resource (the resource name) and dlt/table (the table name, or the resource name when the resource sets the table name in the run).

The default output has no deps, because dlt reads data from outside rivers. To link a resource to the rivers asset that holds its source data, return deps=[rs.AssetDef.dep(...)]. That asset must be in the repository.

items.title: Downstream assets
items.text:
dlt writes the tables to its destination, not to an IO handler. A downstream asset can read the destination, and take the resource's output as a lineage dep:

@rs.Asset(deps=[rs.AssetDef.dep("github_issues")])
def issue_report() -> None: ...

Or it takes the output as an input, through an IO handler that reads the destination. For a DuckDB destination, give the assets a DuckDBIOHandler. The handler reads the table that the duckdb/schema and duckdb/table metadata keys name. Without them, it looks for main.<asset name>, e.g. main.github_issues. So set the keys in the asset_def_fn:

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc
from rivers.integrations.duckdb import DuckDBIOHandler, DuckDBResource

source = github_source()


def asset_def(resource) -> rs.AssetDef:
    metadata = output_def(resource).metadata
    table = source.schema.naming.normalize_table_identifier(metadata["dlt/table"])
    return output_def(
        resource,
        metadata=metadata | {"duckdb/schema": "github", "duckdb/table": table},
    )


github = DltSourceAssets(source, asset_def_fn=asset_def)


@github.assets(
    name="github",
    io_handler=DuckDBIOHandler(resource=DuckDBResource(database="warehouse.duckdb")),
)
def github_assets(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext):
    destination = dlt.destinations.duckdb("warehouse.duckdb")
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline("github", destination=destination, dataset_name="github")
    yield from github.load(context, pipeline)


@rs.Asset
def open_issues(github_issues: pa.Table) -> pa.Table:
    return github_issues.filter(pc.field("state") == "open")

metadata= replaces the default metadata, so asset_def adds the two keys to the dlt/ keys. duckdb/schema is the pipeline's dataset_name, and duckdb/table is the resource's table name. dlt normalizes both names when it loads them: pullRequests becomes pull_requests. normalize_table_identifier does the same for the table name. For the dataset, use a name that does not change, such as github.

The handler loads the resource's root table, e.g. github.issues. dlt loads lists into nested tables, such as issues__labels, and the handler does not read them. When a resource sets its table name in the run, dlt/table is the resource name: set duckdb/table to the table to read.

The IO handler only reads: dlt writes the tables.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• A step runs one pipeline.run, so one failing resource fails the step. For loads that fail on their own, make one DltSourceAssets per group of resources, e.g. with github_source().with_resources("issues").
  • dlt supports Python up to 3.14, and the extra does not install on free-threaded Python.

See the API reference for every parameter.

items.title: DuckDB
items.text:
rivers.integrations.duckdb connects rivers to DuckDB:

  • DuckDBResource opens connections to a database file, MotherDuck, or a DuckLake catalog.
  • DuckDBIOHandler stores each asset as a table, in DuckDB or DuckLake.
  • DuckDBAsset and DuckLakeAsset add maintenance actions.

The Delta Lake handler can also read Delta tables with DuckDB.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
pip install rivers[duckdb]

# Also read Delta tables as DuckDB relations
pip install rivers[delta-duckdb]

items.title: Resource
items.text:
import pyarrow as pa
import rivers as rs
from rivers.integrations.duckdb import DuckDBResource

warehouse = DuckDBResource(database="warehouse.duckdb")

@rs.Asset
def top_users(warehouse: DuckDBResource) -> pa.Table:
    with warehouse.get_connection() as con:
        return con.sql("FROM users ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10").to_arrow_table()

repo = rs.CodeRepository(assets=[top_users], resources={"warehouse": warehouse})

get_connection() closes the connection when the block exits. connect() returns a connection that you close, or that a relation keeps open.

Each call opens a new connection. In one process, DuckDB shares one database instance per file, and releases the file when the last connection closes. A DuckDB file allows one read-write process at a time. When another process holds the file, the resource tries again 10 times, with a delay of 0.1 s that doubles each time (about 100 s in total).

Fields that you do not give are read from DUCKDB_* environment variables, for example DUCKDB_DATABASE.

Field Default Description database ":memory:" A file path, ":memory:", "md:<database>" for MotherDuck, or a DuckLake catalog. connection_config {} DuckDB settings for duckdb.connect(config=...), e.g. {"threads": 4}. extensions [] Extensions to install and load on each connection. secrets {} Secrets to create on each connection: name to CREATE SECRET parameters.

items.title: MotherDuck
items.text:
Set database="md:<database>" and the motherduck_token environment variable:

warehouse = DuckDBResource(database="md:analytics")

items.title: Extensions and secrets
items.text:
lake_files = DuckDBResource(
    extensions=["spatial"],
    secrets={"s3": {"type": "s3", "provider": "credential_chain", "region": "eu-west-1"}},
)

DuckDB loads core extensions such as httpfs, delta, and ducklake when a query needs them.

To run without network access, put the extension files in a directory and point DuckDB at it:

DuckDBResource(
    extensions=["spatial"],
    connection_config={"extension_directory": "/opt/duckdb/extensions"},
)

items.title: IO handler
items.text:
DuckDBIOHandler stores each asset as the table <schema>.<asset name>:

import duckdb
import polars as pl
from rivers.integrations.duckdb import DuckDBIOHandler

io = DuckDBIOHandler(resource=warehouse)

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io)
def orders() -> pl.DataFrame:
    return pl.DataFrame({"day": ["d1", "d1", "d2"], "amount": [5, 7, 3]})

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io)
def daily(orders: duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation) -> duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation:
    return orders.aggregate("day, sum(amount) AS total")

A DuckDBPyRelation input is a lazy query. DuckDB runs it when the output is written, and the rows stream from one table to the other.

Type Write Read duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation yes lazy pyarrow.Table yes eager pyarrow.RecordBatchReader yes lazy arro3 RecordBatchReader yes no polars.DataFrame yes eager polars.LazyFrame yes lazy pandas.DataFrame yes eager

A read needs a type hint on the downstream parameter. Lazy inputs that one step reads share one connection per thread, so the step can join them. A relation that you make with duckdb.sql(...) uses another connection and cannot be joined with the inputs. To query next to the inputs, use warehouse.shared_connection().

Parameter Default Description resource required The DuckDBResource. schema_name "main" The schema for the tables. mode DuckDBWriteMode.OVERWRITE OVERWRITE replaces the table, or the partition's rows. APPEND inserts rows. The strings "overwrite" and "append" work too.

items.title: Partitioned assets
items.text:
Map the partition key to columns with duckdb/partition_expr, as with Delta:

from datetime import datetime

@rs.Asset(
    io_handler=io,
    partitions_def=rs.PartitionsDefinition.daily(start=datetime(2024, 1, 1)),
    metadata={"duckdb/partition_expr": "day"},
)
def events(context: rs.AssetExecutionContext) -> pl.DataFrame:
    ...

An overwrite deletes the partition's rows and inserts the new rows in one transaction. A backfill run with several keys replaces all of them. Daily and hourly keys become ranges, so the column can be text, DATE, or TIMESTAMP.

When two writes conflict, the handler runs the transaction again. It uses DuckLake's retry settings: ducklake_max_retry_count (10), ducklake_retry_wait_ms (100), and ducklake_retry_backoff (1.5). For a DuckLake catalog, change them in connection_config.

items.title: Metadata keys
items.text:
Key Description duckdb/schema Schema for this asset's table. duckdb/table Table name, instead of the asset name. duckdb/mode "overwrite" or "append". duckdb/partition_expr Partition column, or a JSON object from dimension to column. duckdb/columns JSON list of columns to read. duckdb/version DuckLake snapshot to read. ducklake/options JSON object of DuckLake table options.

Each write records duckdb/table, duckdb/num_rows (rows in the whole table), duckdb/write_duration_s, and rivers/schema (with pyarrow or arro3 installed). DuckLake writes also record ducklake/snapshot_id.

items.title: One writer per file
items.text: A DuckDB file allows one read-write process. With the parallel executor or Kubernetes, steps in other processes wait for the file. A lazy input keeps the file open while its step runs. For many writers, use DuckLake with a PostgreSQL catalog.

items.title: DuckLake
items.text:
Pass a DuckLake catalog as the resource's database. The IO handler then writes DuckLake tables:

from rivers.integrations.duckdb import DuckDBIOHandler, DuckDBResource, DuckLake

lake = DuckDBResource(
    database=DuckLake(
        metadata="postgres:dbname=lake host=pg",
        data_path="s3://bucket/lake/",
        options={"expire_older_than": "7 days", "delete_older_than": "7 days"},
    ),
    secrets={"s3": {"type": "s3", "provider": "credential_chain"}},
)
io = DuckDBIOHandler(resource=lake)

The catalog is attached once per process. Each call gets a cursor on that connection. The connection stays open until teardown(), and until the last cursor or relation made from it is gone. Resources with equal fields share it.

DuckLake field Default Description metadata required The catalog database: a DuckDB file path, "postgres:...", or "sqlite:...". data_path None Where DuckLake writes Parquet files. Give credentials for it in secrets. name "lake" The catalog name in SQL. attach_options {} Other ATTACH options, e.g. {"METADATA_SCHEMA": "lake"}. options {} Lake-wide DuckLake options.

items.title: Choose a catalog
items.text:
From Choosing a Catalog Database:

Catalog Clients Use with DuckDB file one process the in-process executor SQLite several local processes, with retries one machine PostgreSQL many, also remote the parallel executor and Kubernetes

A second process that attaches a DuckDB-file catalog fails after the lock retries, with an error that names the limit.

items.title: Tables, snapshots, and data versions
items.text:
• A partitioned asset gets a table that is partitioned by its partition columns. A table that exists is never changed.
  • A partition overwrite is one snapshot.
  • Each write registers the snapshot id as the asset's data version, so downstream assets go stale after a new write.
  • duckdb/version reads an older snapshot. An overwrite of an unpartitioned table keeps the old snapshots readable.
  • DuckLake keeps writes of up to 10 rows in the catalog instead of a Parquet file (data inlining). optimize moves them to files. Change the limit with attach_options={"DATA_INLINING_ROW_LIMIT": n}.

items.title: Conflicts
items.text:
A partition overwrite conflicts with any other write to the same table that commits at the same time (conflict resolution). The handler runs the transaction again with the retry settings above. When many partitions of one table are written at once, limit them with a concurrency pool:

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io, pool="events_table", metadata={"duckdb/partition_expr": "day"})
def events(...): ...

repo = rs.CodeRepository(assets=[events], pool_limits={"events_table": 2})

items.title: Options
items.text:
DuckLake stores options in the catalog. rivers sets an option only when it differs from the stored value. Setting an option makes no snapshot.

  • Lake-wide: DuckLake(options={...}), set when the catalog is attached.
  • Per table: the ducklake/options metadata key, set after each write.
@rs.Asset(
    io_handler=io,
    metadata={"ducklake/options": '{"rewrite_delete_threshold": 0.5, "target_file_size": "128MB"}'},
)
def orders() -> pl.DataFrame: ...

items.title: Maintenance actions
items.text:
from rivers.integrations.duckdb import DuckLakeAsset

class Orders(DuckLakeAsset):
    io_handler = io

    @classmethod
    def materialize(cls) -> pl.DataFrame: ...

repo.run_action("optimize", selection=["orders"])
Class Action What it does DuckDBAsset delete Deletes the partition's rows (with a key) or all rows, and clears the state. A missing table only clears the state. DuckLakeAsset delete The same. DuckLakeAsset optimize Moves inlined rows to files, rewrites files with many deleted rows, and merges small files. Uses the table's rewrite_delete_threshold and target_file_size. DuckLakeAsset vacuum Expires old snapshots and deletes their files, for the whole lake. Uses the lake's expire_older_than and delete_older_than; without them it does nothing.

The actions take no config: the DuckLake options are the settings. A keyed delete needs duckdb/partition_expr.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• The handler writes with overwrite or append. It has no MERGE.
  • DuckDB has no wheels for free-threaded Python or for Linux musl.
  • The Delta reader cannot run on MotherDuck, and reads GCS only with HMAC keys.

items.title: Graph Assets
items.text: Graph assets let you compose multiple Task operations into a sub-DAG that is treated as a single asset in the outer dependency graph. Internal tasks are namespaced as {graph_name}/{task_name} and execute as independent steps in the execution plan.

items.title: When to use graph assets
items.text:
• You have a multi-step transformation that shouldn't be split into separate assets
  • You want to reuse Task functions across different graph assets
  • You need fine-grained control over the execution order within an asset
  • You want internal tasks to use lightweight IO (InMemory) while the graph output uses production IO (Delta Lake)

items.title: Defining tasks
items.text:
A Task is a unit of computation inside a graph asset:

import rivers as rs

@rs.Task
def fetch_data(url: str):
    import requests
    return requests.get(url).json()

@rs.Task
def clean(raw: list):
    return [r for r in raw if r.get("valid")]

@rs.Task(name="enrich", tags=["slow"])
def enrich_data(records: list):
    return [{**r, "enriched": True} for r in records]

items.title: Building a graph asset
items.text:
Use Asset.from_graph() to create a graph asset. Inside the function body, calling tasks records them into a composition graph:

@rs.Asset.from_graph()
def user_pipeline():
    raw = fetch_data("https://api.example.com/users")
    cleaned = clean(raw)
    return enrich_data(cleaned)

The return value determines the graph asset's final node — its output becomes the graph asset's output. Internal tasks are namespaced: user_pipeline/fetch_data, user_pipeline/clean, user_pipeline/enrich.

items.title: Input wiring
items.text:
Task inputs can be wired in two ways:

Positional — pass the output of one task as an argument to the next:

@rs.Asset.from_graph(name="chain")
def chain():
    x = step_a()
    y = step_b(x)       # step_b receives step_a's output
    return step_c(y)

Keyword — explicitly name which parameter receives the value:

@rs.Asset.from_graph(name="chain")
def chain():
    x = step_a()
    y = step_b(x)
    return step_c(value=y)  # only 'value' param is wired from composition

Implicit resolution — task parameters not wired through the composition graph are resolved by name from the outer dependency graph (assets, other tasks):

@rs.Asset
def config_data() -> dict:
    return {"threshold": 0.5}

@rs.Task
def process(value: int, config_data: dict) -> int:
    return value if value > config_data["threshold"] else 0

@rs.Asset.from_graph(name="pipeline")
def pipeline():
    x = compute()
    return process(x)  # 'config_data' is implicitly resolved from the asset

items.title: External dependencies
items.text:
Graph asset functions can accept parameters from the outer dependency graph:

@rs.Asset
def source() -> int:
    return 5

@rs.Asset.from_graph(name="pipeline")
def pipeline(source: int):
    return transform(source)

Assets called inside the graph body keep their bare name (not namespaced) — they are external dependencies, not internal tasks.

items.title: IO handler configuration
items.text:
By default, internal tasks use the same IO handler as the graph asset (or the repository default). Use node_io_handler to give internal tasks a different handler:

@rs.Asset.from_graph(
    name="pipeline",
    node_io_handler=rs.InMemoryIOHandler(),  # internal tasks: fast in-memory
    io_handler=pickle_handler,                # graph output: persisted to storage
)
def pipeline():
    x = step_a()
    return step_b(x)

The final task's output is written through both handlers: node_io_handler for the task itself and io_handler for the graph asset (dual IO write).

Resolution hierarchy for internal task IO handlers:

  1. node_io_handler if set
  2. io_handler if set
  3. Default IO handler from CodeRepository (InMemoryIOHandler)

Both io_handler and node_io_handler accept resource references:

@rs.Asset.from_graph(
    name="pipeline",
    node_io_handler="fast_handler",   # resolved from resources
    io_handler="prod_handler",
)
def pipeline():
    ...

repo = rs.CodeRepository(
    assets=[pipeline],
    resources={
        "fast_handler": rs.InMemoryIOHandler(),
        "prod_handler": pickle_handler,
    },
)

items.title: Executor configuration
items.text:
Use rivers/node/executor metadata to control which executor internal tasks use:

@rs.Asset.from_graph(
    name="pipeline",
    metadata={
        "rivers/node/executor": "in_process",  # internal tasks: in-process
        "rivers/executor": "parallel",         # graph asset step: subprocess pool
    },
)
def pipeline():
    ...

items.title: Why split the executor for the graph and its internals?
items.text:
The two-key split lets you pick isolation/scale at the graph boundary while keeping the internals cheap and traceable. The most useful pattern in production:

  • rivers/executor: "kubernetes" — the graph asset runs as its own pod (its own image, its own CPU/memory request, its own retry boundary).
  • rivers/node/executor: "in_process" — every internal task in that graph runs inside the same step pod, in-process.

You get:

  • Lowest per-task overhead — internal tasks share one Python interpreter, one IO handler instance, one set of resource connections. No fresh pod startup, no container scheduling latency, no extra network round-trips between tasks.
  • Per-graph isolation preserved — the outer pipeline still gets process / pod isolation between graphs; just the inside of each graph collapses into a single execution.

Without rivers/node/executor, internal tasks would inherit the outer executor — under kubernetes, that means each internal task spawns its own step pod. That's right when individual tasks need different images or resources, but excessive for the common case where all tasks in a graph asset are part of the same logical step.

The same pattern works with parallel outside and in_process inside: the graph asset step gets a worker subprocess (avoiding interpreter contention with other graphs), but its internals run synchronously in that subprocess.

items.title: Resolution hierarchy
items.text:
For internal task executor:

  1. rivers/node/executor metadata if set
  2. rivers/executor metadata if set
  3. Job executor or default executor

items.title: Dynamic fan-out
items.text: A task that produces a list (or a list of DynamicOutput) can fan a downstream task out across each element. Each element becomes its own step instance — scheduled, retried, and persisted independently.

items.title: Barrier collect
items.text:
The simplest pattern: produce a list, fan a worker out across it, gather the results back, and pass them to a single downstream task.

@rs.Task
def numbers() -> list[int]:
    return [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

@rs.Task
def double(x: int) -> int:
    return x * 2

@rs.Task
def sum_all(values: list[int]) -> int:
    return sum(values)

@rs.Asset.from_graph()
def doubled():
    nums = numbers()
    mapped = nums.map(double)        # fan out — one `double` instance per element
    return sum_all(mapped.collect())  # barrier — wait for every instance to finish

mapped.collect() blocks until every fanned-out instance has materialized, then yields a single list-typed InvokedNodeOutput you can wire into any downstream task (here sum_all).

items.title: Concurrency cap
items.text:
Pass max_concurrency=N to map to throttle how many instances run in parallel — useful when the fanned-out task hits a rate-limited API or expensive resource:

mapped = ids.map(fetch_record, max_concurrency=4)

Without max_concurrency, the executor schedules instances as eagerly as the outer executor allows.

items.title: Streaming collect
items.text:
When downstream consumption can start before every instance has finished — and especially when results are large — use .collect_stream(). It hands the consumer a generator instead of a list:

@rs.Task
def consume_stream(items: object) -> list:
    return [x for x in items]   # iterate as instances complete

@rs.Asset.from_graph()
def streamed():
    nums = numbers()
    mapped = nums.map(process_item)
    return consume_stream(mapped.collect_stream())

By default collect_stream() emits in completion order; pass ordered=True to emit in mapping-key order instead. Streaming is the right choice when downstream is itself streaming-friendly (a writer, an aggregator) — it avoids buffering the full result set.

The consumer can read one stream from many threads. Each result goes to one thread only.

items.title: Named instances with DynamicOutput
items.text:
By default, fanned-out instances are named with their numeric index (double[0], double[1], ...). When the producer wants stable, human-readable instance names, return a list of rs.DynamicOutput:

@rs.Task
def docs() -> list[rs.DynamicOutput]:
    return [
        rs.DynamicOutput(key="report_q1", value="/data/report_q1.pdf"),
        rs.DynamicOutput(key="report_q2", value="/data/report_q2.pdf"),
        rs.DynamicOutput(key="invoice",   value="/data/invoice.pdf"),
    ]

@rs.Asset.from_graph()
def lengths():
    mapped = docs().map(path_length)
    return sum_all(mapped.collect())

Each instance now runs as lengths/path_length[report_q1], lengths/path_length[report_q2], etc. The name flows into logs, run-event records, and the IO-handler key for that instance — useful when re-runs need to skip already-completed work, or when you want to look up a specific instance in the UI.

DynamicOutput and plain values cannot be mixed in the same producer's list — pick one shape.

items.title: Failure handling
items.text:
When a single mapped instance fails, downstream steps that consume the collect output are skipped (under Executor.parallel()); other instances continue running. The collect step itself ends in failure, propagating to the graph asset's status. This matches normal asset-step failure semantics — fan-out doesn't introduce a new failure mode.

If you cancel the run and some instances do not start, the mapped step also ends in failure. The run ends as Canceled.

items.title: Sharing tasks across graph assets
items.text:
Two graph assets can use the same task — each gets its own namespaced copy with independent wiring and IO:

@rs.Task
def transform(value: int) -> int:
    return value * 2

@rs.Asset.from_graph(name="pipeline_a")
def pipeline_a(source_a: int):
    return transform(source_a)

@rs.Asset.from_graph(name="pipeline_b")
def pipeline_b(source_b: int):
    return transform(source_b)

This creates pipeline_a/transform and pipeline_b/transform as independent steps.

items.title: Using BashTask in graph assets
items.text:
BashTask runs shell commands natively in Rust and can be used inside graph assets:

fetch = rs.BashTask(name="fetch", command="curl -s https://api.example.com/data")

@rs.Task
def parse(raw: str):
    import json
    return json.loads(raw)

@rs.Asset.from_graph()
def api_data():
    raw = fetch()
    return parse(raw)

items.title: Loading graph asset outputs
items.text:
Use repo.load_node() to read outputs after materialization:

repo.materialize()

# Load the graph asset's output (final node's value)
repo.load_node("pipeline")

# Load an internal task's output
repo.load_node("pipeline/step_a")

items.title: Graph assets in jobs
items.text:
When a graph asset is included in a Job, its internal tasks are automatically included:

repo = rs.CodeRepository(
    assets=[pipeline],
    tasks=[step_a, step_b],
    jobs=[
        rs.Job(name="my_job", assets=[pipeline], executor=rs.Executor.in_process())
    ],
)
repo.get_job("my_job").execute()

items.title: Apache Iceberg
items.text: The IcebergIOHandler stores asset outputs as Apache Iceberg tables through a pyiceberg catalog. It writes PyArrow, Polars, pandas, and DuckDB data, partitions tables by the asset's partitions, and supports overwrite, append, and upsert writes, schema evolution, and time travel.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
pip install rivers[iceberg]

# Plus, for these data types:
pip install rivers[iceberg-polars]
pip install rivers[iceberg-pandas]
pip install rivers[iceberg-duckdb]

rivers[iceberg] installs pyiceberg with PyArrow, so PyArrow tables need no other extra. It also installs pyiceberg-core, which pyiceberg needs to write tables that are partitioned by year, month, day, or hour.

The REST catalog needs nothing more. For other catalogs, install the pyiceberg extra of the catalog, for example pyiceberg[sql-postgres], pyiceberg[sql-sqlite], pyiceberg[glue], or pyiceberg[hive].

items.title: Basic usage
items.text:
import polars as pl
import rivers as rs
from rivers.io_handlers.iceberg import IcebergIOHandler

io = IcebergIOHandler(
    catalog_name="lake",
    catalog_properties={"type": "rest", "uri": "https://catalog.example.com"},
    namespace="analytics",
)

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io)
def users() -> pl.DataFrame:
    return pl.DataFrame({
        "id": [1, 2, 3],
        "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"],
    })

The first write creates the namespace and the table analytics.users.

items.title: Catalogs
items.text:
The handler loads the catalog with pyiceberg.catalog.load_catalog(catalog_name, **catalog_properties). pyiceberg also reads the properties of the catalog from .pyiceberg.yaml and from environment variables (see Storage), so the handler can use a catalog that you configure outside your code:

io = IcebergIOHandler(catalog_name="lake", namespace="analytics")

A local catalog for development and tests needs pip install "pyiceberg[sql-sqlite]":

io = IcebergIOHandler(
    catalog_name="local",
    catalog_properties={
        "type": "sql",
        "uri": "sqlite:////data/iceberg/catalog.db",
        "warehouse": "file:///data/iceberg/warehouse",
    },
    namespace="dev",
)

The handler loads the catalog for each read and write, and keeps no catalog object, so it also works in the worker processes of Executor.parallel().

items.title: Table names
items.text:
Each asset writes the table {namespace}.{asset name}. Two metadata keys change the name for one asset:

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io, metadata={"iceberg/namespace": "raw", "iceberg/table": "events_v2"})
def events() -> pa.Table:
    ...

Dots in a namespace make a nested namespace: namespace="lake.raw" is the namespace raw in lake. REST catalogs can create tables in nested namespaces. pyiceberg's SQL catalog cannot.

items.title: Storage
items.text:
The storage settings and credentials of the table files are pyiceberg FileIO properties. pyiceberg reads them from the catalog properties, so put them in catalog_properties. They apply to every table of the catalog:

io = IcebergIOHandler(
    catalog_name="lake",
    catalog_properties={
        "type": "sql",
        "uri": "postgresql+psycopg2://user:password@db/catalog",
        "warehouse": "s3://bucket/warehouse",
        "s3.endpoint": "http://minio:9000",
        "s3.access-key-id": "...",
        "s3.secret-access-key": "...",
        "s3.region": "us-east-1",
    },
    namespace="analytics",
)

The keys are pyiceberg's, not the storage_options keys of the Delta handler: s3.access-key-id, not AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID. Frequently used keys:

Store Keys S3 and S3-compatible stores s3.endpoint, s3.access-key-id, s3.secret-access-key, s3.session-token, s3.region, s3.force-virtual-addressing Azure (ADLS) adls.account-name, adls.account-key, adls.sas-token, adls.tenant-id, adls.client-id, adls.client-secret Google Cloud Storage gcs.project-id, gcs.oauth2.token

Without credentials, pyiceberg uses the default credential chain of the store, for example the AWS environment variables, profile, or instance role.

To keep the credentials out of your code, set them in .pyiceberg.yaml, or in environment variables named PYICEBERG_CATALOG__<CATALOG>__<KEY>. In the key, write __ for each . and _ for each -:

export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__LAKE__S3__ACCESS_KEY_ID=...
export PYICEBERG_CATALOG__LAKE__S3__SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...

pyiceberg reads a _ in the catalog name as - too, so these variables cannot configure a catalog named my_lake. Use a name without _, such as my-lake.

A REST catalog can give out short-lived credentials for each table, and pyiceberg asks for them by default. pyiceberg uses these credentials before the catalog properties, so with such a catalog you often set no storage keys.

All readers and writers use the same properties:

  • pyiceberg reads and writes the files for writes, and for PyArrow and pandas inputs.
  • Polars inputs: polars converts the S3 keys, the Azure keys, and gcs.oauth2.token for its own reader.
  • DuckDB inputs: the handler turns the S3 and Azure keys into a DuckDB secret (see Read with DuckDB).

items.title: Supported types
items.text:
Type Extra Read with pyarrow.Table rivers[iceberg] a pyiceberg scan, into memory pyarrow.RecordBatchReader rivers[iceberg] a pyiceberg scan, in batches polars.DataFrame rivers[iceberg-polars] pl.scan_iceberg, collected polars.LazyFrame rivers[iceberg-polars] pl.scan_iceberg, lazy pandas.DataFrame rivers[iceberg-pandas] a pyiceberg scan, into memory duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation rivers[iceberg-duckdb] DuckDB's iceberg_scan, lazy

The type of the returned value selects the writer. The type annotation of the downstream parameter selects the reader.

About writes:

  • A write needs memory for all of its data. pyiceberg 0.12 also reads a RecordBatchReader or a DuckDB relation into memory.
  • Iceberg v2 stores timestamps in microseconds, and pyiceberg accepts only UTC time zones. The handler writes nanosecond timestamps as microseconds, and zoned timestamps as UTC.
  • The pandas index is not written.

items.title: Read with DuckDB
items.text:
A duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation input reads the table's current metadata file with DuckDB's iceberg_scan. The relation is lazy. iceberg/columns, the partition predicate, and file statistics prune the files that DuckDB reads. iceberg/snapshot_id reads an older snapshot.

import duckdb
import rivers as rs

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io)
def summary(orders: duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation, users: duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation) -> duckdb.DuckDBPyRelation:
    return orders.join(users, "user_id").aggregate("country, sum(amount) AS total")

Inputs that one step reads share one DuckDB connection per thread, so the step can join them. To set extensions, secrets, or settings, pass a DuckDBResource as handler_config={"duckdb": DuckDBResource(...)}.

The handler turns the table's storage properties into a DuckDB secret for the table's bucket or container. These properties include the credentials that a REST catalog gives out for the table.

  • S3 (s3.*, with client.* as fallback): the access key, secret, session token, region, endpoint, and s3.force-virtual-addressing. Without a key, DuckDB uses the AWS credential chain.
  • Azure (adls.*, for abfs:// and abfss:// tables): an account key, a SAS token, or a service principal. Without one, DuckDB uses the Azure credential chain.
  • GCS: not supported. DuckDB reads GCS only with HMAC keys; set them with DuckDBResource(secrets=...).

items.title: Write modes
items.text:
Set the default mode on the handler, or change it for one asset with metadata:

io = IcebergIOHandler(catalog_name="lake", namespace="analytics", mode="append")

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io, metadata={"iceberg/mode": "overwrite"})
def events() -> pl.DataFrame:
    ...
Mode Behavior overwrite Replace the table, or the rows of the partition (the default) append Add rows upsert Update the rows that match on the join columns, and insert the others

Each write is one commit: schema changes, table properties, and data. When another writer commits first, pyiceberg tries the commit again, 4 times by default. Set the number with the commit.retry.num-retries table property, for example when many partitions of one table are written at the same time.

items.title: Upserts
items.text:
from rivers.io_handlers.iceberg import IcebergIOHandler, UpsertConfig

io = IcebergIOHandler(
    catalog_name="lake",
    namespace="analytics",
    mode="upsert",
    upsert_config=UpsertConfig(join_cols=["id"]),
)

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io, metadata={"iceberg/join_cols": '["order_id"]'})
def orders() -> pa.Table:
    ...
  • join_cols are the columns that identify a row. Without them, pyiceberg uses the table's identifier fields.
  • UpsertConfig(when_matched_update_all=False) only inserts new rows. UpsertConfig(when_not_matched_insert_all=False) only updates rows.
  • The data must not have two rows with the same join columns.
  • Rows that did not change are not written. When no row changes, the write makes no snapshot and the data version stays the same, so downstream assets do not become stale.
  • An upsert matches rows in the whole table. For a partitioned asset, put the partition column in the join columns.
  • An upsert does not change the schema. Add new columns with an overwrite or append write and schema_mode first.

items.title: Schema evolution
items.text:
schema_mode Behavior None (default) A write with a new column fails. A column that the data does not have is written as nulls. "merge" Add new columns and widen types before the write "overwrite" Also delete the columns that the data does not have. Needs mode="overwrite".

Set it on the handler or with the iceberg/schema_mode metadata key. A type change that Iceberg cannot widen, for example from long to string, fails.

items.title: Partitioned writes
items.text:
Combine with PartitionsDefinition and iceberg/partition_expr:

@rs.Asset(
    io_handler=io,
    partitions_def=rs.PartitionsDefinition.daily(start=datetime(2024, 1, 1)),
    metadata={"iceberg/partition_expr": "ts"},
)
def events() -> pl.DataFrame:
    ...

iceberg/partition_expr names the column of the partition. For multi-partitions, it is a JSON object from dimension name to column:

metadata={"iceberg/partition_expr": json.dumps({"region": "region", "day": "event_date"})}
  • An overwrite replaces only the rows of the partition. A backfill run with many partition keys replaces the rows of all its keys.
  • When the table is partitioned on the same columns, pyiceberg drops the data files of the partition. Otherwise it rewrites the files without the partition's rows.
  • A partitioned input reads only the rows of its partition.
  • On date and timestamp columns, the partition is a time range. On other columns, such as strings, the keys are compared as text in the partition key format.

The first write creates the table with a partition spec from the asset's partitions:

Partition dimension Column type Iceberg transform Static or dynamic any identity Time window timestamp the coarsest of year, month, day, hour that all windows align to Time window date the coarsest of year, month, day that all windows align to Time window other identity

For example, daily partitions on a timestamp column give day(ts), hourly partitions give hour(ts), weekly partitions give day(ts), and monthly partitions give month(ts). The handler never changes the partition spec of a table that exists.

items.title: Table and snapshot properties
items.text:
io = IcebergIOHandler(
    catalog_name="lake",
    namespace="analytics",
    table_properties={"write.parquet.compression-codec": "zstd"},
    snapshot_properties={"producer": "rivers"},
)

@rs.Asset(
    io_handler=io,
    metadata={
        "iceberg/table_properties": '{"commit.retry.num-retries": "10"}',
        "iceberg/snapshot_properties": '{"team": "growth"}',
    },
)
def events() -> pl.DataFrame:
    ...
  • Table properties are set when the table is created, and set again when they change. Properties that you remove from the config stay on the table.
  • Snapshot properties are added to the summary of each snapshot that the handler writes.

items.title: Reading data
items.text:
Downstream assets read the data by type annotation:

@rs.Asset(io_handler=io)
def summary(users: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return users.group_by("region").len()

The metadata of the upstream asset selects the table and its partitions. An input with its own metadata, from AssetDef.input(..., metadata=...), uses that metadata instead. So repeat the upstream keys that the read needs, such as iceberg/partition_expr.

items.title: Column selection
items.text:
@rs.Asset(
    io_handler=io,
    deps=[rs.AssetDef.input("users", metadata={"iceberg/columns": '["id", "name"]'})],
)
def user_names(users: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    ...

items.title: Time travel
items.text:
Each write records its snapshot id as iceberg/snapshot_id in the materialization's metadata. iceberg/snapshot_id on an input reads that snapshot:

@rs.Asset(
    io_handler=io,
    deps=[rs.AssetDef.input("users", metadata={"iceberg/snapshot_id": "4720155209217613612"})],
)
def users_at_release(users: pa.Table) -> pa.Table:
    ...

items.title: Output metadata and data versions
items.text:
Each write records iceberg/table, iceberg/mode, iceberg/snapshot_id, iceberg/num_rows and iceberg/size_bytes (of the whole table), iceberg/write_duration_s, iceberg/metadata_location, and rivers/schema. An upsert also records iceberg/rows_updated and iceberg/rows_inserted.

The snapshot id is the asset's data version. A write that changes the table makes a new snapshot, so downstream assets become stale.

items.title: Maintenance actions
items.text:
Subclass IcebergAsset to get the delete and expire_snapshots actions. They use the asset's IcebergIOHandler: the same catalog, table, and snapshot properties as the writes.

from rivers.io_handlers.iceberg import IcebergAsset  # also exported as rs.IcebergAsset

class Orders(IcebergAsset):
    io_handler = LAKE

    @classmethod
    def materialize(cls) -> pl.DataFrame:
        return pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3]})


repo = rs.CodeRepository(assets=[Orders])
repo.run_action("expire_snapshots")
repo.run_action("expire_snapshots", config={"assets": {"orders": {"config": {"retention_hours": 24}}}})
repo.run_action("delete", partition_key=pk)
Verb Declaration Behavior delete Unmaterialize + Exclusive + DownstreamFirst + Optional key Deletes the rows of the partition, or every row without a key. A keyed delete needs iceberg/partition_expr. expire_snapshots Unchanged + Exclusive + Keyless Removes old snapshots from the table's metadata.

expire_snapshots takes two config fields:

  • retention_hours: expire the snapshots that are older. The default is the table's history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms property, 5 days by default.
  • retain_last: always keep this many of the newest snapshots of the table's history. The default is the table's history.expire.min-snapshots-to-keep property, 1 by default.

Branch and tag heads are never expired. pyiceberg removes only the snapshots: their data files stay in storage. pyiceberg cannot compact files or remove orphan files yet, so IcebergAsset has no optimize or vacuum. Use an engine such as Spark for those.

On a table that does not exist yet, expire_snapshots reports unchanged, and delete still applies Unmaterialize, so the asset's state clears. A subclass that defines a verb replaces the built-in one.

items.title: Custom verbs
items.text:
For other verbs, the handler gives action bodies the table and the partition filter that the writes use:

class Events(IcebergAsset):
    io_handler = LAKE

    @classmethod
    def materialize(cls) -> pl.DataFrame: ...

    @rs.action(outcome=rs.Outcome.Unchanged)
    @classmethod
    def tag_release(cls, ctx: rs.ActionContext) -> None:
        table = ctx.io_handler.load_table(ctx.asset_name, ctx.asset_metadata)
        table.manage_snapshots().create_tag(table.current_snapshot().snapshot_id, "release").commit()
  • load_table(asset_name, asset_metadata): the pyiceberg Table, with the iceberg/namespace and iceberg/table overrides.
  • partition_filter(asset_metadata, partition, schema): the pyiceberg expression for the rows of the partition, with iceberg/partition_expr.
  • resolved_snapshot_properties(asset_metadata): the snapshot properties of the asset's commits.

items.title: Migrating from Dagster or Prefect
items.text:
rivers ships an agent skill that teaches AI coding agents how to port a Dagster or Prefect project to rivers: the concept mapping, the exact API surface, and the places where a mechanical translation would silently change behavior.

The skill lives in skills/migrate-to-rivers/ in the rivers repository.

items.title: Why a skill
items.text: rivers is young enough that models invent its API when asked to write it from memory — plausible names like PartitionsDefinition.static(...) or MetadataValue.float(...) that do not exist. The skill pins the agent to a signature-exact reference generated from the type stubs, and gives it a porting workflow with validation gates, so a migration fails loudly instead of producing code that looks right.

items.title: Install
items.text:
Claude Code (plugin)Any agent (copy) 
/plugin marketplace add ion-elgreco/rivers
/plugin install rivers@rivers

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/ion-elgreco/rivers /tmp/rivers
mkdir -p .claude/skills
cp -r /tmp/rivers/skills/migrate-to-rivers .claude/skills/

Agents other than Claude Code can read SKILL.md and the files in references/ directly — they are plain markdown with no tool-specific syntax.

items.title: Use
items.text:
Point your agent at the project you want to port:

Migrate the Dagster project in ./pipelines to rivers

The skill takes over from there: it inventories the source project, maps concepts, ports bottom-up (resources and IO handlers, then assets, partitions, automation, jobs), and validates each slice with repo.validate() before moving on.

items.title: What it covers
items.text:
Dagster Prefect Assets / ops / tasks ✅ ✅ Multi-assets, graph assets ✅ ✅ Partitions & partition mappings ✅ n/a Automation conditions ✅ ✅ (from triggers) Schedules & sensors ✅ ✅ (from deployments) IO managers → IO handlers ✅ ✅ (from result storage) Resources / config ✅ ✅ (from Blocks) Retries, concurrency, executors ✅ ✅

Dagster maps closely — rivers uses the same asset model, so most definitions have a direct counterpart. Prefect maps loosely: its flows are imperative and rivers' graph is declarative, so the skill treats those ports as design work and asks rather than guessing.

items.title: What it will tell you it cannot do
items.text:
The skill is written to report gaps instead of approximating them. Expect it to flag:

  • Asset checks — no rivers equivalent; assertions must move into the asset body
  • Integration packages — dagster-aws and friends have no rivers ports; dagster-slack maps to rivers.integrations.slack, dagster-duckdb (with its pandas and polars IO managers) to rivers.integrations.duckdb, dagster-airbyte to rivers.integrations.airbyte, dagster-datadog to rivers.integrations.datadog, dagster-pandera to pandera return hints, checked by rivers.integrations.pandera, dagster-sling to rivers.integrations.sling, dagster-databricks (its client resource, the run-now and submit-run ops, and the workspace component, without Pipes) to rivers.integrations.databricks, dagster-dlt to rivers.integrations.dlt, dagster-iceberg (its PyArrow, Polars, and pandas IO managers) to rivers.io_handlers.iceberg, and dagster-dbt to rivers.integrations.dbt, where dbt tests gate the models they test instead of becoming asset checks
  • Prefect caching — cache_policy / cache_key_fn have no direct analog; rivers uses materialization state, code_version, and data_version instead
  • Dynamic control flow — Prefect flows whose shape depends on runtime data do not fit a declarative DAG
  • Cloud-only features — Dagster+ and Prefect Cloud functionality

items.title: Keeping it honest
items.text: Every rivers snippet in the skill's reference files is exercised by python/tests/test_migration_skill.py, which runs against the built extension. If an API is renamed, the test fails and the skill gets updated with it.

items.title: pandera
items.text: rivers.integrations.pandera validates asset outputs against pandera schemas. Give an asset a pandera return hint, and rivers checks each frame that the asset returns.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
pip install rivers[pandera,pandas]   # pandas frames
pip install rivers[pandera,polars]   # polars frames

You do not import the integration: rivers finds it from the return hint.

items.title: Validate an asset's output
items.text:
Annotate the return with pandera.typing.DataFrame[Model]:

import pandas as pd
import pandera.pandas as pa
from pandera.typing import DataFrame, Series

import rivers as rs

class Orders(pa.DataFrameModel):
    """Orders placed in the shop."""

    id: Series[int] = pa.Field(ge=0, unique=True, description="Order id")
    amount: Series[float] = pa.Field(gt=0, nullable=True)
    status: Series[str] = pa.Field(isin=["open", "closed"])

@rs.Asset
def orders() -> DataFrame[Orders]:
    return pd.read_parquet("orders.parquet")

When the asset returns, rivers calls schema.validate(frame, lazy=True). A valid frame is stored and recorded. An invalid frame fails the step with AssetOutputValidationError, and nothing is stored. Downstream assets do not run.

These return hints hold a schema:

Return hint Value pandera.typing.DataFrame[Model] pandas.DataFrame pandera.typing.polars.DataFrame[Model] polars.DataFrame pandera.typing.polars.LazyFrame[Model] polars.LazyFrame Annotated[pd.DataFrame, schema], Annotated[pl.DataFrame, schema] The frame, checked against schema: a DataFrameSchema object or a DataFrameModel class DataFrame[Model] \| None A frame, or None (not validated)

A value of the wrong type, for example a dict for DataFrame[Orders], fails like any other return type check.

items.title: Polars
items.text:
import polars as pl
import pandera.polars as pa
from pandera.typing.polars import DataFrame, LazyFrame

class Orders(pa.DataFrameModel):
    id: int = pa.Field(ge=0)
    status: str = pa.Field(isin=["open", "closed"])

@rs.Asset
def orders() -> DataFrame[Orders]:
    return pl.read_parquet("orders.parquet")

@rs.Asset
def open_orders(orders: pl.DataFrame) -> LazyFrame[Orders]:
    return orders.lazy().filter(pl.col("status") == "open")

pandera checks a LazyFrame for its columns and types only, so that the frame is not collected. To also check its rows, set PANDERA_VALIDATION_DEPTH=SCHEMA_AND_DATA.

items.title: DataFrameSchema objects
items.text:
A DataFrameSchema cannot be a type argument. Put it in Annotated:

from typing import Annotated

orders_schema = pa.DataFrameSchema(
    {"id": pa.Column(int, pa.Check.ge(0)), "status": pa.Column(str)},
    name="Orders",
)

@rs.Asset
def orders() -> Annotated[pd.DataFrame, orders_schema]:
    return pd.read_parquet("orders.parquet")

rivers first checks that the value is a pd.DataFrame, then validates it against the schema.

items.title: The stored frame
items.text:
rivers stores the frame that pandera returns, not the frame that the asset returned. This makes the schema options that change data take effect in storage: coerce, add_missing_columns, drop_invalid_rows, column defaults, and parsers.

class Prices(pa.DataFrameModel):
    price: Series[float]

    class Config:
        coerce = True

@rs.Asset
def prices() -> DataFrame[Prices]:
    return pd.DataFrame({"price": [1, 2]})  # stored with price as float64

items.title: Schema metadata
items.text:
Each validated materialization records the schema as pandera/schema, a JSON MetadataValue. The UI shows it with the other metadata of the materialization:

{
  "name": "Orders",
  "description": "Orders placed in the shop.",
  "columns": [
    {"name": "id", "type": "int64", "nullable": false, "unique": true, "description": "Order id", "checks": ["greater_than_or_equal_to(0)"]},
    {"name": "amount", "type": "float64", "nullable": true, "unique": false, "description": null, "checks": ["greater_than(0)"]},
    {"name": "status", "type": "string[pyarrow]", "nullable": false, "unique": false, "description": null, "checks": ["isin(['open', 'closed'])"]}
  ],
  "checks": []
}

A pandera/schema entry that the asset sets itself, with context.add_output_metadata() or Output(metadata=...), replaces this one.

items.title: Failures
items.text:
Validation is lazy, so the error lists every failed check, not only the first. The message has pandera's report:

AssetOutputValidationError: Asset 'orders' returned a value that does not match 'pandera.typing.pandas.DataFrame[pipeline.Orders]': {
    "DATA": {
        "DATAFRAME_CHECK": [
            {
                "schema": "Orders",
                "column": "id",
                "check": "greater_than_or_equal_to(0)",
                "error": "Column 'id' failed element-wise validator number 0: greater_than_or_equal_to(0) failure cases: -1"
            },
            ...
        ]
    }
}

Both executors validate the same way. The parallel executor validates a sync step in its worker process.

To turn validation off, set pandera's PANDERA_VALIDATION_ENABLED=False. rivers then stores the frame as the asset returned it.

items.title: Multi-asset outputs
items.text:
A multi-asset has one return hint for all its outputs. Give an output its own hint with AssetDef(type_hint=...). rivers validates that output's frame the same way as a returned frame:

@rs.Asset.from_multi(
    output_defs=[
        rs.AssetDef("orders", type_hint=DataFrame[Orders]),
        rs.AssetDef("refunds"),
    ]
)
def load():
    yield rs.Output(read_orders(), output_name="orders")
    yield rs.Output(read_refunds(), output_name="refunds")

An invalid frame fails its output. See Return type checks for the other outputs.

items.title: Inputs
items.text: rivers validates return values, not inputs: a frame is validated once, when its asset writes it. Annotate a downstream parameter with the frame type, for example orders: pd.DataFrame. DeltaIOHandler and DuckDBIOHandler read by that type and do not accept a pandera hint there.

items.title: From dagster-pandera
items.text:
Dagster rivers pandera_schema_to_dagster_type(Model) with @asset(dagster_type=...) or Out(dagster_type=...) Return hint DataFrame[Model] AssetOut(dagster_type=...) in @multi_asset AssetDef(name, type_hint=DataFrame[Model]) pandera_schema_to_dagster_type(schema) for a DataFrameSchema Return hint Annotated[pd.DataFrame, schema] Failed TypeCheck AssetOutputValidationError with pandera's report The type's schema metadata (a TableSchema) pandera/schema metadata on each materialization

Dagster checks the frame and keeps the frame that the asset returned. rivers keeps the frame that pandera returns.

items.title: Partitioned Assets
items.text: This guide walks through practical partition patterns. See Partitions concept for API details on PartitionsDefinition, PartitionKey, and PartitionMapping.

items.title: Static partitions with Delta Lake
items.text:
Partition by a fixed set of categories and map each to a Delta Lake column:

import rivers as rs

partitions = rs.PartitionsDefinition.static_(["us", "eu", "asia"])

@rs.Asset(
    partitions_def=partitions,
    io_handler=io,
    metadata={"delta/partition_expr": "region"},
)
def regional_data():
    ...

The delta/partition_expr metadata tells the IO handler which column maps to the partition dimension. On read, the handler generates a predicate (region = 'us').

Execute a specific partition:

repo = rs.CodeRepository(assets=[regional_data])
repo.materialize(partition_key=rs.PartitionKey.single("us"))

# Multiple partitions at once
repo.materialize(partition_key=rs.PartitionKey.single(["us", "eu"]))

items.title: Time-window partitions with Delta Lake
items.text:
Time-window partitions generate range predicates on read (date >= '2024-01-15' AND date < '2024-01-16'):

from datetime import datetime

partitions = rs.PartitionsDefinition.daily(start=datetime(2024, 1, 1))

@rs.Asset(
    partitions_def=partitions,
    io_handler=io,
    metadata={"delta/partition_expr": "date"},
)
def daily_events():
    ...
